📍🇯🇵 Kyoto, Japan

Today our guide taught us the Japanese concept of “ichi-go ichi-e” which translates to “one lifetime, one encounter,” serving as a reminder that every single moment and gathering is entirely unique and can never be replicated. To come to Kyoto during cherry blossoms season really captures this for me, it’s incredibly crowded but you can only truly have this experience in this one week window, and it will never be exactly the same even if you came back. Right before we left I saw an article from Travel and Leisure saying “skip Kyoto and go here instead” for Cherry Blossom. Who writes this shit? That’s like saying “skip going to the Super Bowl and go watch the local high school play”. Even if you didn’t come during cherry blossom season Kyoto is a 10/10, I plan to come back to Japan at some point and see everywhere else, but this was an incredible experience.

📍🇯🇵 Kyoto, Japan

The Arashiyama Bamboo Grove in Kyoto offers a surreal experience where towering stalks of green bamboo create a natural cathedral, filtering sunlight into a soft, ethereal glow that dance across the forest floor. At the northern edge of the grove lies Tenryu-ji Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage site founded in 1339 by the shogun Ashikaga Takauji to venerate Gautama Buddha and appease the spirit of Emperor Go-Daigo. The area’s history is deeply rooted in the Heian Period (794–1185), when it served as a favored retreat for Japanese aristocrats who sought the tranquil beauty of the Oi River and the surrounding mountains. Today, the “Sound of the Bamboo” the rhythmic creaking and rustling of the stalks, is officially recognized by the Japanese Ministry of Environment as one of the 100 Soundscapes of Japan, preserving the spiritual and historical stillness that has defined Arashiyama for centuries.

📍🇯🇵 Tokyo, Japan 

Tokyo during cherry blossom season is definitely an experience worth doing. Tomorrow we head to Kyoto.

📍🇯🇵 Tokyo, Japan

We had a lot of fun in Tokyo, it’s hard to comprehend how big it is, you can ride the subway for 30 minutes and only be a few neighborhoods over from where you started. 

Tokyo’s cherry blossom season, which typically peaks between late March and early April, transforms the city into a sea of pink and white, centered around iconic “hanami” (flower-viewing) spots like Ueno Park, Shinjuku Gyoen, and the Meguro River. This tradition dates back to the Heian period (794–1185), when it was initially an aristocratic pastime before spreading to the common people during the Edo period. Major locations like Ueno Park became famous after the third Tokugawa shogun, Iemitsu, transplanted trees there from Mount Yoshino, while the rows of cherry trees along the Sumida River were reportedly planted by the eighth shogun, Yoshimune, to both provide a public recreation space and help reinforce the riverbanks through the footsteps of visitors. Today, these historical sites remain at the heart of the season, showcasing the Somei-yoshino variety, which was actually developed in Tokyo’s own Somei village in the mid-19th century, as a fleeting symbol of renewal and the ephemeral nature of life.

📍🇨🇴 Medellín, Colombia

Colombia is special, it’s rare for me to visit anywhere twice, I’ve only done it for Mexico and Costa Rica in Latin America, but the country just had so much to offer. I think South America is just this constant state of contradictions; it’s chaotic and laid back all at the same time. When I came here in 2015, everyone asked the same question “Is it safe?”, it’s a fair question, but very outdated, Pablo Escobar has been dead since 1993, and the issues stemming from him have been over for decades. Once you realize that you’ll understand Colombia has a lot to offer; natural beauty, vibrant cities, incredible food and culture, and amazing people.

Colombia is a vibrant South American country shaped by a complex history that blends Indigenous civilizations, Spanish colonization beginning in the 16th century, independence led by figures like Simón Bolívar, and a more recent era marked by internal conflict and remarkable economic and cultural resurgence. Its culture reflects a rich fusion of Indigenous, African, and Spanish influences, expressed through music such as cumbia and vallenato, colorful festivals, and a deep sense of regional pride. Colombian cuisine is hearty and diverse—dishes like arepas, bandeja paisa, ajiaco, and fresh Caribbean seafood showcase local ingredients ranging from Andean potatoes to tropical plantains. The capital, Bogotá, sits high in the Andes and serves as the political and cultural heart of the nation, known for its historic La Candelaria district and world-class museums. Medellín, once infamous for cartel violence, has transformed into an innovative, forward-looking city celebrated for its eternal spring climate and urban development. On the Caribbean coast, Cartagena enchants visitors with its colonial walled city, vibrant plazas, and centuries-old fortifications, standing as a testament to Colombia’s strategic importance during the Spanish Empire.

📍🇨🇴 Medellín, Colombia 

Enjoy this time lapse as a storm rolls in over the mountains. 

Medellín is Colombia’s second-largest city, nestled in the lush Aburrá Valley and known as the “City of Eternal Spring” for its mild, year-round climate. Once infamous for cartel violence associated with Pablo Escobar in the 1980s and early 1990s, Medellín has since transformed into one of Latin America’s most innovative urban centers. The city is celebrated for its pioneering public transportation system—especially its cable cars connecting hillside neighborhoods—vibrant street art in Comuna 13, thriving tech and startup scene, and rich paisa culture. Visitors are drawn to landmarks like Plaza Botero, filled with sculptures by hometown artist Fernando Botero, as well as the city’s lively food scene, coffee culture, and annual Flower Festival (Feria de las Flores).

📍🇫🇮🇸🇪🇩🇰🇫🇷🇮🇹🇨🇭🇨🇷🇩🇪🇧🇪🇳🇱

2025 was good to us, I’m eternally optimistic and think 2026 will be even better. Going to Japan 🇯🇵 in March for the Cherry Blossom 🌸 then Taiwan 🇹🇼 Singapore 🇸🇬 Malaysia 🇲🇾 and Thailand 🇹🇭 that summer. Oktoberfest 🇩🇪 🍻 🥨 and the Dolomites 🇮🇹 ⛰️ in September, then I’m not too sure the rest of the year. Id like to go to China 🇨🇳 and Hong Kong 🇭🇰 and probably Guatemala 🇬🇹 but nothing planned after September.

📍🇩🇪🇧🇪🇳🇱🎅🏻🎄

If there is one trip I’d recommend for a kid, it’s Europe during the Christmas Market season. It just feels exactly like what Christmas is supposed to feel like, and it’s simply magical for them. We hit Cologne 🇩🇪 Brugge, Ghent, Antwerp 🇧🇪 and Amsterdam 🇳🇱 over 10-days, all great and each offering something slightly different and special. I’ve been to about 25 different Christmas Markets, and hands down Prague, Czech Republic 🇨🇿 is my favorite. It’s the only one I’ve done twice, it is simply perfect. After that, in no particular order, these are my other favorites: Vienna, Austria 🇦🇹 Strasbourg, France 🇫🇷 Ansbach and Nuremberg, Germany 🇩🇪 Budapest, Hungary 🇭🇺

Christmas markets in Europe trace their origins to the late Middle Ages, when winter fairs in German-speaking lands allowed towns to stock up on food and crafts before Christmas; over centuries, these markets evolved into seasonal celebrations of light, warmth, and local identity. What makes them special is how each city expresses the same tradition through its own food and atmosphere: in Nuremberg, the air is filled with the smell of Nürnberger bratwurst and Lebkuchen; nearby Ansbach, rooted in Franconian beer culture, pairs its intimate baroque square with hearty sausages and dark winter beers, often including smoked Rauchbier. Strasbourg, often called the “Capital of Christmas,” reflects Alsatian heritage with flammekueche, bredele cookies, and spiced vin chaud, while Vienna’s imperial markets emphasize refinement, offering punsch, roasted chestnuts, sausages, and pastries beneath grand architecture. In Prague, Gothic backdrops frame stalls selling trdelník, ham roasted on spits, and hot mead, creating a medieval feel, while Budapest blends Central European flavors with lángos, goulash, chimney cake, and mulled wine along the Danube. Together, these markets transform winter into a shared ritual—where regional food, history, and community turn cold nights into something festive.

📍🇳🇱 Amsterdam, Netherlands 

Sometimes I just put on music and wander around with no particular plans or direction in mind. I’ll stop for coffee or lunch, maybe taste 6 different cheese stores samples. Before you realize you’ve walked 25-miles through Amsterdam in 2-days. 

Amsterdam rose to prominence in the late Middle Ages and especially during the 17th-century Dutch Golden Age as one of the world’s most important trading cities. As the hub of the Dutch East India Company and home to the world’s first modern stock exchange, it helped pioneer global trade, finance, and capitalism. From Amsterdam, Dutch commercial power extended to colonized and controlled territories including Indonesia (the Dutch East Indies), parts of the Caribbean such as Curaçao and Aruba, Suriname in South America, trading posts in India and Sri Lanka, the Cape Colony in South Africa, and New Netherland in North America (including present-day New York City). These colonies and trade networks allowed Amsterdam to shape global commerce by linking Europe to Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

📍🇧🇪 Antwerp, Belgium 

Merry Christmas from the City of Diamonds, Antwerp, Belgium. 

At Christmastime, Antwerp glows with warmth and tradition, especially around the Cathedral of Our Lady, where festive markets fill the historic squares with lights, mulled wine, and the scent of waffles. The cathedral itself, a UNESCO World Heritage site, anchors the city’s medieval heart and reflects Antwerp’s golden age as one of Europe’s most important trading ports. Antwerp has been at the heart of the global diamond trade for over 500 years, dating back to the early 15th century, and today nearby districts still handle the majority of the world’s rough and polished diamonds. This blend of seasonal charm, Gothic grandeur, and commercial legacy gives Antwerp a uniquely luminous atmosphere during the holidays.

📍🇧🇪 Ghent, Belgium

Ghent is a solid place to spend an afternoon on Christmas Eve. 

Ghent is a historic Flemish city known for its medieval architecture, winding canals, and powerful role as a trade and textile center in the Middle Ages. Landmarks like Gravensteen Castle and St. Bavo’s Cathedral reflect centuries of prosperity and cultural influence. At Christmas, Ghent transforms with festive lights and markets that blend historic charm with cozy winter traditions. The Christmas markets are especially loved for warm treats like freshly fried beignets and indulgent melted raclette sandwiches enjoyed against the backdrop of the old city.

📍🇧🇪 Brugge, Belgium

Somewhere in my memory is this time I went to Brugge with this other couple about 13 years ago and they fought the whole time, and at one point the wife told the husband to “shut the fuck up.” True story. Corcovado National Park, on Costa Rica’s remote Osa Peninsula, is often described as one of the most biologically intense places on Earth, offering a rare glimpse of wildlife thriving in an almost completely untouched environment. Its remoteness is a defining feature—most visitors can only access the park by boat or on long, challenging hikes, with the famed Sirena Ranger Station serving as the heart of the experience deep within the rainforest. This isolation protects an extraordinary density of wildlife: all four of Costa Rica’s monkey species, scarlet macaws, herds of peccaries, vibrant poison dart frogs, crocodiles, and larger, harder-to-see species like Baird’s tapirs, giant anteaters, and even jaguars and pumas. The combination of difficult access, vast stretches of primary rainforest, and minimal human presence makes Corcovado not just a national park but one of the last truly wild places in Central America.

Venice, founded over 1,500 years ago on a lagoon of islands, developed a rich culinary tradition shaped by its role as a powerful maritime republic and gateway between East and West. As Venetian merchants brought back spices, grains, and exotic ingredients from across the globe, these influences blended with the city’s local bounty—especially seafood from the Adriatic. A beloved expression of this heritage is cicchetti, bite-sized snacks traditionally served in bacari (rustic wine bars) since at least the 13th century. Originally enjoyed by workers and traders seeking a quick, affordable bite with wine, cicchetti include classics like baccalà mantecato (creamed cod), fried calamari, or crostini topped with salumi and vegetables. Today, this tradition remains central to Venetian life, offering a flavorful, social way to experience the city’s history through its food.

Bologna, a historic city in northern Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region, is renowned for its rich cultural heritage, vibrant food scene, and one of the oldest universities in the world. Founded by the Etruscans and later expanded under Roman rule, Bologna became an influential medieval city, especially after the establishment of the University of Bologna in 1088. This institution attracted scholars from across Europe and helped shape Bologna into a hub of intellectual and legal thought. During the Renaissance, the city flourished artistically and economically, despite periods of Papal control. Bologna’s well-preserved medieval architecture, such as the Two Towers (Asinelli and Garisenda), its arcaded streets, and red-tiled roofs, continue to reflect its nickname “La Rossa” (The Red), symbolizing both its architecture and leftist political history. Today, Bologna blends academic tradition, culinary excellence, and vibrant urban life, standing as a testament to its enduring legacy.

The nation is primarily divided into three main language sectors: the German-speaking region, which is the largest and covers central and eastern Switzerland, including cities like Zurich, Bern, and Basel; the French-speaking region in the west, known as Romandy, which includes Geneva, Lausanne, and Neuchâtel; and the Italian-speaking region in the south, primarily located in the canton of Ticino and parts of southern Graubünden. 📍🇲🇦 Fés, Morocco 

The Chouara Tannery in Fés, Morocco, is one of the city’s most iconic landmarks and a testament to its centuries-old leatherworking tradition. Established in the 11th century, it is the largest and oldest tannery in Fes and operates much as it did during medieval times. The tannery is located in the heart of the Fes el-Bali medina, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and features a vibrant array of stone vats filled with natural dyes and solutions.

The leather tanning process begins with raw hides, which are cleaned and softened using a mixture of water and lime. Workers then dye the leather using natural pigments such as saffron, indigo, and henna. The process is labor-intensive, performed entirely by hand, and produces high-quality leather that is crafted into bags, shoes, and other goods sold in the surrounding souks.

Visitors can observe the tannery from nearby terraces, where the sight of colorful dye pits and the scent of the process create an unforgettable sensory experience. Despite its pungency, the Chouara Tannery remains a must-see for its authentic glimpse into Morocco’s cultural heritage.

An iconic landmark located on the northern bank of the Tagus River in Lisbon, Portugal. Built between 1514 and 1520 during the reign of King Manuel I, the tower originally served as part of the city’s defensive system and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon. Designed in the Manueline style, it features ornate maritime motifs, intricate carvings, and unique elements like armillary spheres, ropes, and crosses of the Order of Christ.

A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983, it is celebrated for its historical significance, architectural beauty, and stunning location, offering visitors panoramic views of the river and surrounding area.

•Giving Birth•
It has to be the most excruciating pain I’ve ever felt going through natural birth. 😫

Thanks to this experience, I can never see mother the same ways anymore. 

•Recovery•
Due to the difficult birth, apart from tearing, my uterus was hanging out dangling like an upside down mountain 😩 (ya apparently it can happen, no kidding) 
Haemorrhoids hated me too 😆 swell to a thumb size from all that pushing.
I spend more than a month in laying position to eat and rest.
Honestly looking back it’s crazy how much and how hard my body have to work to recover even though I’m still not 100% yet.

•Parenthood•
As the saying goes, “It takes a village to raise a child.” I don’t exactly have a village nor my local food. So it’s been at times really hard and miserable. Dav always said, I have him in which I’m very thankful for. Nevertheless it’s different and very hard.
Dav and I are both very sleep deprived which is no surprise, however our hearts are very full seeing our Eddie smile and grow.

All in all, I’m thankful to be a mum and most importantly, Eddie’s mum. 🩵

Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery by mending the areas of breakage with urishi lacquer dusted or mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. This actually reinforces the pottery and makes it stronger and more beautiful than ever. Kintsugi is seen as a metaphor for healing in grief and beauty in brokenness. 

So many times in my life I felt broken, beaten, and defeated by storms that came my way. But each time, God picked me up and put me back together, making me whole again, and more resilient for the next storm. His power is made perfect in my weakness. What others might see as flaws, He sees something beautiful. 

My main character, Shinju, definitely goes through the process of Kintsugi. She is crushed, but perseveres, and emerges stronger than she ever thought she could be.

Alas… Chase Atlantic slipped through my fingers again🙃 In a manic panic, I Googled the vinyl and every website took me to a 404 error page, SOLD OUT. Even with my @duolingo teachings, my ability to read in Japanese was not good enough to purchase a copy from Japan, ばか!!!!😡
A few hours later, a STRANGER remembers seeing my fb post more than a day ago. They send me a link that I hadn’t come across, BEHOLD- Resist Records still had copies!!!🤩 I managed to snag my new holy grail and for CHEAPER than advertised anywhere else, before thanking my saviour🎉 Side note: they picked a very questionable press “milky white” swipe to see and you’ve got one guess at what I’m calling it💦
This was the story of buying one of my favourite albums of all time, hope this took you on a journey🤪

As a landlord, you have a responsibility to follow the rules and stay compliant, especially when it comes to evictions.

There’s a myth that evictions in this city have to take 60-90 days. The truth is if you actually follow the legal steps for a non-payment case, you can have it wrapped up in about 5 weeks.

The Steps:
1️⃣ 3-Day Notice: Must be served correctly or your case is dead on arrival.
2️⃣ Filing: Head to the Clerk of Courts. It’s $110 for one tenant and $7 for each additional guest.
3️⃣ Court Day: Show up and have your paperwork ready.
4️⃣ The Set-Out: If they aren't gone, the move-out happens within 7 days.

Keep it professional, keep it legal, and keep it moving! 💯✊

Hallo! I'm Joanna of Coral Pea Designs. This business and my career as a watercolour artist is now a year old. This is my garden, where I have spent a lot of my time, between the pandemic and being bed & housebound for a year due to losing my muscles to Hyperemesis Gravidarum, a complication of my pregnancies. A lot of my paintings have been of plants photographed by my sister in law, Dr Laura Skates @floraskates, which helped me feel like my world was still connected when I was too weak to walk across a room. I am grateful that I can now share my joy of local plants with others through my painting.

If you want to learn more about what I do, you can ask in the comments, send me a DM for a chat or check out the link in my bio.

Small tattoos don’t always mean easy tattoos! There’s a lot that goes into making sure a tiny portrait still reads well and holds up over time.

Der Post ist natürlich nur meine persönliche Meinung, ich selber habe jedoch die Erfahrung gemacht, dass mich die Energie und Connection zum Artist am Tag des Termins immernoch begleitet bei den Tattoos, die ich selber habe. Das kann extrem positiv sein, in dem ein oder anderen Fall aber auch total schade, wenn die Erfahrung vor Ort nicht gut war. 

Am Ende ist es natürlich auch immer eine Frage der Persönlichkeiten beider Personen. Termine mit mir zum Beispiel verlaufen meistens eher ruhig und beim Tätowieren (und tätowiert werden😁) rede ich relativ wenig. Ich glaube für manche Menschen wirkt das entspannend und ich hoffe auch immer, dass es richtig verstanden wird, aber ich bin beim Tätowieren super konzentriert und allgemein glaube ich nicht so besonders gut in Small-Talk. Aber ich versuche beim Tätowieren immer ganz viel positive Energien und Gedanken in euer Tattoo fließen zu lassen, damit ihr kraftvolle Begleiter an eurer Seite habt! Klingt vielleicht esoterisch, aber naja, vielleicht ist es auch einfach die jahrtausendealte Tradition die aus mir spricht 🙂‍↕️😁

Was ist euch wichtig während einem Termin, damit ihr euch wohl und gesehen fühlt? Hattet ihr schon besonders positive oder negative Erlebnisse?

Hatte diese Serie schon länger in meinen Zeichnungen. Ich könnt jedes der Ornamente anfragen.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Heute fühle ich mich nur noch selten so, und wenn ich bedenke, dass ich mich letztes Jahr zu dieser Zeit noch in der Tagesklinik befunden habe kann ich mittlerweile sagen, dass ich einen echt weiten Weg gekommen bin. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
In der Klinik erhielt ich die Diagnose Borderline und plötzlich ergab vieles Sinn. Gleichzeitig wusste ich eigentlich rein garnichts darüber, hatte nur Vorurteile in meinem Kopf von manipulativen, toxischen „Monstern“, die Menschen verletzen und die so quasi der Antichrist der psychischen Störungen seien. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Mittlerweile verstehe ich die Krankheit besser und weiß, dass das natürlich ziemlich an der Realität vorbeigeht. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Denn eigentlich ist die tragische Ironie an der Krankheit, dass zwischenmenschliche Connection, Liebe, Geborgenheit, also Dinge die Menschen zum (Über)leben benötigen, uns als Kind genommen oder nie mitgegeben wurden. Das, was wir uns am allermeisten auf der Welt wünschen, ist gleichzeitig auch das, was uns am allermeisten Angst macht. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
So jagen wir etwas hinterher, das wir uns so sehnlichst und verzweifelt wünschen, und wenn wir es bekommen, halten wir es nicht aus. Oder Kappen Bindungen, aus Angst verlassen zu werden, verletzen uns auf verschiedenste Weisen selber, gehen ausbeuterische Beziehungen ein um ein Stück Liebe zu bekommen, leben in einem ständigen Alarmzustand der Gefühle. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Es ist wirklich ein harter Kampf, Heilung zu erreichen. Borderline gilt als die am schmerzhaftesten zu ertragende psychische Krankheit mit der höchsten Su*z*drate.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Aber, und das geht gerade an dich solltest du auch die Diagnose haben: die Krankheit ist keine Endstation. Mit den richtigen Maßnahmen wird es besser! Therapien, sich Informieren und Selbsthilfegruppen, Wahrnehmung und Akzeptanz der eigenen Gefühle, sowie Arbeiten am Selbstwert haben mir extrem geholfen. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀

Seit 15 Jahren die dicksten Kartoffeln 🥔❤️‍🔥

„Aber es ist doch ‚nur‘ eine Linie?!“ bekomme ich öfter mal als Reaktion nach einer Anfrage auf mein Angebot. Da blutet mir immer etwas das Herz, denn gerade perfekte Linien und Ringe stellen mit das Anspruchsvollste dar, was man sich tätowieren lassen kann. 

Daher nehme ich euch heute mal mit durch einen Termin! Zuerst zeichne ich die Linie in mehreren Gängen Freihand an, um eine möglichst genaue Vorlage zu erzielen. Ich arbeite hier ohne Stencil, was ein in meinen Augen noch besseres Ergebnis erzielt und eventuelle Ecken durchs Anlegen vermeidet. 

Danach tätowiere ich ganz vorsichtig die Linie und arbeite mich auch hier vorsichtig in meist mehreren Durchgängen nach vorne. Ich sag’s euch wie es ist, in den ersten Jahren meiner Karriere hatte ich vor solchen Tagen echt schlaflose Nächte. Denn was wäre schlimmer, wenn man eine gerade Linie anfragt und am Ende eine Sinuskurve am Arm hat? (Nothing personal Sinuskurven, ihr seid super 😄)

Nun, nach 8 Jahren tätowieren, bringe ich so viel Routine mit, dass mir diese Termine immer leichter von der Hand gehen und allgemein liebe ich ja eh die Herausforderung, Dinge möglichst perfekt zu machen ;) bedenkt also, dass wenn ihr ein Motiv wie dieses anfragt, ihr auch und vor allem für die Jahre an Lernen,  Expertise und die ruhige Hand bezahlt, die es benötigt, es am Ende so clean und simpel aussehen zu lassen.

When I met a friend yesterday, she and her talked about being self-employed or even entrepreneurs as women* and and how it is like, to be frequently underestimated, frequently assumed that there has to be a „partner“ doing this with us, the expectations being higher in so many situations as if we were men leading a company and at the same time basically handling our struggles alone most of the time, because if you have a look around… mostly, in our position, it’s men. It still is. I sometimes forget this because I work with almost only self-employed women around me. But actual… that’s pretty rare. 

And it got clear to me again that even now that I’ve built and working in a studio almost completely run by women, I can’t escape being put in a role, or making assumptions or being tried to be exploited just because I’m female passing in so many situations. 

Best example: hiring handymen for studio renovations. I went from being nice to being not really nice anymore because chances are super high someone tries to rip me off if I’m just nice to them. 

Can we just stop doing this? Start seeing people as people, treating everyone with respect, start giving everyone the same chances… can’t be so hard? Why do we still have to fight for these things? 

At the same time I’m thankful that my problems are „only“ this where I live, that people can go on the street here and that we have come a long way. My thoughts go out to all women* on earth who still have to fight for their basic human rights in their lives. 

I hope you had a good day everyone 🤍

Det känns så futtigt att försöka klä känslorna i ord. Det räcker liksom inte till.
Allt det där vi växte upp med, alla fina ord om ”aldrig igen” och alla människors lika värde osv osv…det var bara tomma ord.
Vi ser det nu. Varje dag på skärmarna på våra telefoner.
Vi ser människor slitas i stycken, brännas och svältas till döds, jagas, förnedras och skuldbeläggas.
Det här är ingen ”tragisk händelse”, det är ett massmord, finansierat och orkestrerat.
Så gott som alla världens regeringar är medskyldiga eftersom det bara fortsätter och fortsätter.
I FN pratar man. Och pratar. Och pratar.
I Sverige väljer vår regering, istället för att agera för att förhindra det här fruktansvärda, att försöka lägga någon slags skuld på de som protesterar.
Man utmålar demonstranter som demokratiskt fientliga, klär dem i ord som ”odjur”, samtidigt som man stöttar de värsta odjuren.
Och hatet i kommentarsfälten tycks inte ha något slut…

Jag måste övertyga mig själv om att vi är fler än dem, för det här kan inte vara de vi är. Det får inte vara så.

I usa regerar fascisterna. En fet och sinnesförvirrad president håller tal som inte innehåller något, uppmanar militären att slåss mot sin egen befolkning och i Sverige sneglar vi på detta land som någon slags förebild.
Jag har bott i usa. 13 år av mitt liv bodde jag där och överallt jag kom fick jag höra att Sverige verkade vara ett så fantastiskt land. Och det var det. För när jag växte upp hade vi ledord som ”solidaritet”, ”medmänsklighet”, ”demokrati”.
Det Sverige som världen såg upp till var ett annat land än det vi lever i nu.
När jag jobbade på Wholefoods blev en tjej på mitt team mamma. Hon hade två veckors mammaledighet.
Sverige är bättre än så. Det borde vara det. 
Valet nästa år är förmodligen det viktigaste vi haft i min livstid.

Så. Nu kör jag på Patreon och ni är varmt välkomna att följa mig där.

Jag som inte ens kan teckna.
Det känns så - jag har ingen aning om vad jag håller på med, tecknar inte av objekt, jag känner mer som att jag avbildar former och mönster i olika färger och när jag är klar har det blivit en bild, eller en avbildning av något.

Jag var 15,eller 16 när jag började med konst, fast jag tycker inte om att säga att jag gör konst, jag var extremt skoltrött och ville ingenting. Men det var ju det där med gymnasiet, man måste ju plugga vidare och bli något.
Min morsa, som själv drömde om att måla, teckna, skriva och skapa, men som pga livet aldrig kunde göra det ”på riktigt”, mer eller mindre tvingade mig att söka till Bild o Form i Hässleholm där vi bodde då.
Hon förstod att jag inte behövde mer av den vanliga skolan och hon såg till att jag fick ihop de arbetsprover som behövdes. Jag kan inte tänka mig att de var särskilt bra…men jag kom in på skolan.
Och det ändrade allt.
Det var 1991 och jag har fortsatt teckna sedan dess, mer eller mindre aktivt, men det har alltid funnits i mitt liv.
Och det är jag oändligt tacksam för.

Less chaos. More margin. More family dinners.
More peace.

Families aren’t asking for luxury - they’re asking for a life that doesn’t require sacrificing their health, marriage, or time with their kids just to survive.
We’re not broken.
The system is.

50yrs THIS WEEK….Normally i would whinge about being so old but when i look back on my youth i have lived through some of THE most prosperous decades of rock n’ roll that are NEVER to be repeated so i CANT complain…Like THIS week !!! On March 15, 1976, the New York quartet released Destroyer, their fourth studio album and the record that transformed them from cult, live circuit favorites into arena-conquering legends. Half a century later, Rolling Stone (i WAS a good rag back then), STILL ranks it among the 500 greatest albums of all time, and the fans who grew up with it couldn’t agree more.

The timing of Destroyer was everything. Three years of relentless touring and theatrical live shows had built a fanatical following, but it was the band’s 1975 live album Alive!, which spent 110 weeks on the Billboard chart and became their first gold-certified record, that finally cracked open the mainstream. Riding that momentum, KISS turned to producer Bob Ezrin, fresh off his acclaimed work with Alice Cooper, to help them make their most ambitious studio record yet. The lineup reads like a greatest-hits collection all on its own: the thunderous “God of Thunder,” the anthemic “Shout It Out Loud” and the soft-rock ballad “Beth,” which became the band’s first top-10 single, peaking at No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100. Destroyer itself peaked at No. 11 on the Billboard 200 and was eventually certified double platinum by the RIAA, the first KISS album to reach that milestone. For ME it was their PEAK everything….Popularity, performance & presence !!! Introducing their ICONIC Kiss Alive II stage set-up, which was a FIRST of its kind AND of course their iconic outfits…..!!!! This was them at their biggest & fucking best. That era marked them as the BIGGEST band in music & the atmosphere at that time was magnetic….WHAT A TIME !!!!! My fav standout tracks are Sweet Pain & Flaming Youth ⭐️ #rockandroll #rock #metal #kiss #beer ☠️☠️☠️

Most mums I talk to have been quietly Googling “postnatal depression symptoms” at 2am because something feels off but the word “depression” doesn’t quite fit.

Matrescence is the psychological term for the identity shift that happens when you become a mother. It’s as significant as adolescence. And almost nobody is told it exists.

That doesn’t mean it’s never postnatal depression. Sometimes it is, and that’s important to recognise too. But for a lot of mums, what they’re experiencing isn’t a disorder. It’s an enormous transition that nobody prepared them for.

The difference matters. Because if you think you’re broken, you try to fix yourself. If you know you’re in a transition, you can start making sense of it. You can understand what’s shifting, sit with it, and process it instead of fighting it.

None of this means something is wrong with you. It means something is happening to you. And it helps to have someone in your corner who can help you figure out which one it is.

I cannot focus when my house is a mess. Not “oh it’s a bit annoying” - like, my brain literally won’t work.

So today I hired someone to come and sort out the toys and the bookshelf because I knew I was never going to get to it properly on my own.

And honestly? Walking into a tidy playroom just made everything feel lighter.

I know it won’t last (she’s already pulling things out as I type this). But getting it off my mental load, even temporarily, was worth every dollar.

Not everyone can hire someone, and that’s okay. Maybe it’s asking your partner to do one specific thing, swapping a playdate for a tidy-up session with a friend, or just tackling one corner instead of the whole house. The point is the same: you don’t have to carry it all yourself.

What’s the one thing in your house that does your head in? Mine is the kids’ toys, every single time.

Then I walked past and saw them. Just sitting there. Playing. Not fighting. Not needing me. Just two little humans being gentle with each other.

Nobody told me motherhood would be this specific mix of being completely wrecked and completely in love in the same hour.

The build-up is so gradual you don’t even notice it’s happening.

One rough night becomes ten. One skipped meal becomes a pattern. You stop noticing that you haven’t sat down without someone on you since the morning.

Your body starts keeping score before your mind catches up:

🔹 The tight chest that won’t ease
🔹 The jaw clenching you don’t notice until midday
🔹 Snapping over something small and then feeling guilty about it

The rage that shows up out of nowhere. Not a bad mood. Actual fury, often directed at your partner, and you don’t even know why. That’s HCG and oestrogen, and it’s far more common than people admit.

The brain fog. Forgetting what you walked into the room for. Losing words. Feeling like you’ve lost ten IQ points. Your brain is actually pruning and rebuilding neural pathways to prepare you for motherhood. It’s not you going mad; it’s your brain reprioritising.

The sensory overload. Sounds are louder. Smells are unbearable. Being touched feels like too much. Your nervous system is becoming more alert, and sometimes it overshoots.

And the ones nobody talks about: intrusive thoughts about something terrible happening to your baby. Feeling disconnected from your bump when you expected to feel bonded. Quietly grieving the person you were before, even when you’re happy about the baby.

None of this means something is wrong with you. But it does mean you deserve more than a five-minute check-up that only asks about your blood pressure.

If no one’s talking to you about this stuff, follow along.

The six-week check-up is supposed to be about you. But most of the time, it barely scratches the surface.

You get ten minutes. You get asked if you’re coping (and what are you supposed to say to that?). You get a contraception chat. And then you’re cleared. Like the whole thing is done.

But it’s not done. Not even close.

Nobody mentions that your mood can dip months after the birth, not just in the early weeks. Nobody checks whether you’re actually eating, sleeping, or being supported. Nobody asks if the thoughts you’re having at 2am are frightening you. And even if they hand you a screening questionnaire and you tick all the “right” boxes, that doesn’t mean you’re okay. A score on a form can’t capture what’s actually going on inside you.

And nobody says the thing that matters most: six weeks is not the finish line. Recovery takes as long as it takes. For some women that’s months. For others it’s a year or more. And the hardest stretch often comes after the fourth trimester, when the world has moved on and you’re still in it.

You are allowed to still be recovering. You are allowed to need more support than a ten-minute appointment. You are allowed to not be fine yet.

If this is where you are right now, save this. And send it to a mum who needs to hear that she’s not behind.

When you’re completely fried as a mum, sometimes the best reset is the one you least expect.

So I checked. And honestly? It helped. Not in a “fixed everything” way. In a “my jaw unclenched and I stopped snapping at everyone for five minutes” way.

You know those days. You’ve been up since 5. The baby’s been unsettled all morning. You’ve been touched constantly since the moment you opened your eyes. You haven’t finished a hot drink. You haven’t finished a thought. Your shoulders are up around your ears and you don’t even realise until someone asks if you’re okay and you nearly cry.

Then the kids put music on. And they start dancing. And something in your body just shifts.

Movement and music pull your nervous system out of fight-or-flight. Even 30 seconds of it. Your breathing slows. The knot in your chest loosens. You’re still exhausted, but the edge comes off.

I’m a psychologist and this is genuinely one of the simplest things I recommend. Not because it’s a cure. Because it interrupts the spiral long enough to come back to yourself. I love it every time I try it. 

So next time you’re about to lose it, put something on. Dance badly in your lounge room while the washing pile judges you from the couch. Your toddler won’t even notice; they’re too busy doing their own moves.

The most common thing people say to a new mum is “let me know if you need anything.”

And the most common thing a new mum does is never ask.

Not because she doesn’t need help. Because she’s too exhausted to figure out what to ask for, too proud to feel like a burden, or too deep in survival mode to even know what she needs.

So don’t wait to be asked.

Bring food. Real food, not snacks. Text “I’m dropping something at your door at 2pm” instead of “do you need anything?” Keep your visit to 30 minutes and only longer if the mum seems to be enjoying your company. Ask about her, not just the baby. Fold the laundry without asking. Load the dishwasher on your way out.

The mums who feel most supported aren’t the ones with the most visitors. They’re the ones whose people showed up without being asked.

Nobody talks about the moment your nervous system just stops coping. 

Not the tiredness. Something deeper than that. When the noise, the touching, the feeding, the broken sleep all stack up until your body simply cannot take in any more.

That's maternal overstimulation. 

And it's one of the most common, least talked about experiences of new motherhood.

It happens because your nervous system is already working overtime. Hormonal shifts after birth, sleep deprivation and the constant physical demands of a newborn all lower your threshold for what you can handle. Things that felt manageable before baby now feel completely overwhelming. 

That's not weakness. That's biology.

Your body isn't failing you. It's sending you a signal that you need rest, space and support.
You're not dramatic. You're not weak. You're a new mum whose nervous system is doing its absolute best.

Three years ago, I became a mother.

And every year when this day comes around, I don’t just celebrate you…
I remember your birth.

I remember the room.
The feeling in my body.
The moments that stayed with me long after we left the hospital.

I remember feeling like things were happening to me, not with me.

Because birth doesn’t end when the baby is born.

It stays with you.

It lives in your body, in your memories, in the way you tell the story.

Grounding.
Something they carry with pride.

For others, it feels heavy.
Unresolved.
Like something was taken from them.

And that matters.

and how deeply birth experiences shape that.

A positive birth doesn’t mean perfect.
It means feeling heard, respected, safe, and supported.

Because when those things are missing…
it doesn’t just disappear.

It follows you into motherhood.

Into your confidence.
Your nervous system.
Your memories of the day everything changed.

Three years on, I’ve done a lot of reflecting, a lot of healing, and a lot of learning.

And it’s a big part of why I care so deeply about the work I do now.

Because how a woman feels in her birth… matters long after the birth is over.

🗣️ Postpartum is not a 6 week finish line - it’s a journey that takes time, support, and understanding.

The 6 week postnatal check up often feels like a quick tick box exercise that hands us a ‘green light’ to bounce back, but the reality is so different. Healing is not linear, and it definitely doesn’t end at 6 weeks.

👉🏼 Research shows that postpartum recovery takes at least 12 months - sometimes even longer - to fully process the physical, mental, and emotional changes that come with motherhood. From hormones to mental health to pelvic floor recovery - it all takes time.

Let’s talk about this. Let’s redefine postpartum as a season of healing - not a deadline. ❤️

If you’ve been searching for tips on baby self soothing, this video is your reminder to take a deep breath.

The truth? True baby self soothing is a developmental milestone. Infants don’t have the neurological wiring to calm their own nervous systems yet. What they actually need is responsive parenting, a caregiver who lends their calm to soothe the baby’s storm.

And yet somehow, we’ve been told the opposite.

That a baby who cries when mum leaves is “too attached.”
That picking them up every time creates bad habits.
That needing you is a problem you caused.

It isn’t. Here’s what the research actually says:

🧠 Bowlby’s attachment theory shows that seeking a caregiver when distressed is a biological survival mechanism.

🧠 Separation distress is developmentally normal from infancy through toddlerhood, it peaks between 9 and 18 months but remains developmentally normal through age three.

🧠 Thomas and Chess’s landmark temperament research found that every baby is born with their own innate temperament and their own way of experiencing the world.

🧠 Responsive parenting in the early years is what builds the neural pathways for independent self soothing later.

So the next time someone tells you your baby is too clingy or too attached, remember that you are not spoiling them.

You are doing exactly what your baby needs.

Follow for more baby psychology research, translated into language that actually makes sense for parents. 🧠

#babydevelopment #babyselfsoothing #babytemperament #responsiveparenting #babypsychology

Somewhere along the way, baby sleep became something to fix. And it feels sleep training is the sole solution.

Rocking to sleep? Dependency.
Contact naps? A bad habit.
Co-sleeping, nursing to sleep? You’re making it worse.

But here’s what the science of baby sleep actually tells us:

🫶🏻 Attachment researcher John Bowlby (1969) established that a baby’s need for physical closeness is a biological survival mechanism hardwired into human development.

🔬Decades later, biological anthropologist James McKenna at the University of Notre Dame’s Mother-Baby Sleep Lab showed that maternal proximity actively regulates infant breathing, heart rate, and arousal during sleep.

📜 Archaeologists have found 4,000 year old lullaby incantations describing mothers using touch, rhythm, and movement to soothe their babies.

Across every culture, for thousands of years, rocking, holding, and tapping was simply how babies slept. Not a problem. Not a habit to break. A biological response to a nervous system that isn’t yet able to regulate on its own.

The concept of sleep training - teaching babies to sleep without physical support is just decades old.

You are not creating a problem. You are meeting a need.

No one prepared you for the baby sleep advice that was coming.

From the moment a mother gives birth - before anyone asks about her postpartum recovery - she will be asked: “how is the baby sleeping?” “Are they sleeping through the night yet?”

Sleep train. Don’t sleep train. Bad habits. Wake windows. And somehow through all of it, you are left wondering what you did wrong.

Nothing. You did nothing wrong.

The research on baby sleep tells a very different story to what most parents are handed. Studies consistently show that night waking is statistically normal well beyond the first year. How easily a baby self-settles is largely temperament, NOT a result of your choices.

If your baby is not sleeping through the night, that is not evidence of failure. It is evidence of a developing nervous system doing exactly what it is supposed to do.

The baby sleep industry is worth billions. Your sleep deprivationhas been turned into a product. In a world of completely unregulated sleep advice, the most radical thing you can do is trust the baby sleeps research over the noise.

Your baby’s sleep is not a measure of your worth as a mother.

Giving birth is the moment I lost my old self. 
Here are 5 things I want you to know about that - from a postpartum perspective no one talks about. 👇

1. Your postpartum recovery journey won’t be linear. One day you’ll feel whole, one day you might feel completely broken. Both are part of the process. And it’s not 6 weeks! Postpartum recovery can take up to 2 years.

2. It’s okay to grieve your old self. Missing who you were before doesn’t mean you don’t love your baby. Or that you’re failing as a mother. Both can coexist. it is one of the most normal and least discussed experiences in early motherhood.

3. The worst advice anyone will give you after giving birth is “you’ll get back to yourself again.” Your body carried a human being. Your mind rebuilt itself around a new life. She isn’t lost. She EVOLVED. Looking for the old version will only keep you from meeting the new one.

4. What you are going through has a name and it’s called matrescence - the neurological, hormonal and psychological transformation a woman goes through when she becomes a mother. Your brain literally rewires itself. It was identified in 1973 and we still barely talk about it.

5. When someone asks “how can I help?” and you go blank that’s not you being difficult. Your nervous system is in survival mode. Your mental load is at capacity. You are not supposed to have the answer. The people around you are supposed to show up anyway.

Giving birth will change you life.
Postpartum is not a phase to push through. Share it with a postpartum mum who needs it🤍

#givingbirth #realmotherhood #mothersday #postpartum #newmum

It’s not a baby behaviour problem.
It’s baby development.
And yet everyone will try to give you parenting advice.

Here's why some babies can’t stop even when you’ve said “no” ten times.

This baby behaviour study at the University of Maryland by researcher Dr. Amy Hane observed two 9 month old babies.
Both babies were told not to touch the plant.
🔬 Emily heard “no” once. She moved on.
🔬 Jack kept going back. Again and again. His mother had to work twice as hard just to keep up.

🧠 This is called a highly reactive temperament.
Jack’s nervous system is wired to respond strongly to stimulation.

What the researchers did next says everything about baby development:
👉🏻 They didn’t correct Jack more
👉🏻 They didn’t raise their voice
👉🏻 They removed the plant
Because with a highly reactive baby -
the environment needs to adapt to them.
Not the other way around.

💡 If you have a Jack:
Before you repeat yourself again,
ask what you can remove from the room.
Not what you can say differently.

This isn’t a baby behaviour problem.
It’s a temperament difference.
And understanding baby development
changes everything about how you parent.

💬 Do you have a Jack or an Emily?

The contact nap isn’t just for your baby.
Sometimes you need her weight on your chest more than she needs yours.

In a world that films what mums do the second their baby sleep - the dishes, the emails, the to-do list - we’ve forgotten something important.
Rest is not laziness. It is postpartum recovery.

Here’s what psychology actually says about contact naps:

🧠 Physical touch triggers oxytocin - the bonding hormone that calms your nervous system, not just your baby’s

😮‍💨 Skin-to-skin contact lowers cortisol, your body’s stress hormone.

🤝 Contact naps are co-regulation in its most natural form. Your nervous systems are quite literally regulating each other

💤 Contact naps are not a bad habit and won’t ruin your baby sleep routine.

Our modern society praises the productive nap time. The mum who ticks off her list while her baby sleeps. But no one talks about the mum who simply needed to stop.

We’ve turned baby sleep into a performance. Into proof that you’re doing it right. But contact naps were never the problem, the unrealistic expectations were.

So the next time a contact nap runs longer than planned - let it.

And if this resonates, this page is for you - psychology informed, judgement-free motherhood content every week.

☝️ Most couples argue more in postpartum not because of incompatibility - but because of overwhelm.
This isn’t a relationship problem.
It’s part of postpartum journey no one prepares us for.
And the moment you understand that, you can meet each other with compassion instead of conflict.

You’re not falling apart - you’re in the hardest chapter of becoming parents together.

I never planned to give birth 
with no epidural.

That’s my birth story. 
I just kept going, moment by moment, until there was no other way through.
And what I learned in that birth room - no birthing class could have taught me.

One thing I want to address. Birth plans matter. Education matters. I went to classes, I knew my options, I understood what could happen.

These are the 5 psychology-based truths that protected my mental health while starting daycare:

1️⃣ Tears = Secure Attachment. (Ainsworth)
She protests because I am her safe haven. Securely attached children prefer their primary caregiver. Baby crying at separation isn’t damage - it’s connection.

2️⃣ Separation anxiety = A cognitive milestone. (Piaget)
Around 18-20 months, object permanence becomes stronger. She now understands I exist even when I’m out of sight. She is not regressing - she is developing.

3️⃣ The hug = The repair. (Tronick)
Attachment isn’t built on perfect goodbyes. It’s built on mismatch and repair. The reunion is what strengthens the bond.

4️⃣ Play = Progress. (Bowlby)
Success isn’t a tear-free morning. It’s exploration. She can be sad at the door and still activate her exploratory system once she feels safe.

5️⃣ My gut = My power. (Bandura)
Parental self-efficacy means I trust myself. If starting daycare ever stops feeling right, I can adjust the plan.

Starting daycare is hard.
But the science is clear:

Your bond is bigger than a heartbreaking baby crying at drop off. 🤍

This is your reminder ⤵️

Postpartum care is not just about the baby.
It’s about the mother, too.

Your body is healing.
Your hormones are shifting.
Your nervous system is recalibrating.
Your identity is changing.

And all of that affects postpartum mental health - on a wide spectrum.

For some, that looks like exhaustion, overwhelm, or emotional overload.
For others, it can include experiences like postpartum depression.

None of it is a personal failure.
And none of it is fixed by being harder on yourself.

Real postpartum care,
real postpartum support looks like compassion.
Rest.
Warm meals.
And permission to move slower in a season that asks so much of you.

Postpartum is not a weakness.
It’s a season of recovery.

And you deserve care while you’re in it 🤍

I never planned an unmedicated birth. 

Here’s what I learned while giving birth moment by moment:

1️⃣ Not having a birth plan was the BEST decision because it helped me stay flexible.
Education is important - I knew the options that might be offered to me.

Having a fixed plan would have anchored my brain to one outcome.
Birth is deeply mental, and flexibility mattered more than control.

2️⃣ I wouldn’t have known I could stand.
If my midwives hadn’t encouraged me to stand and move during contractions, I probably would’ve stayed on the bed a simply because that’s what we’re used to seeing.
Standing and moving actually helped me cope better with contractions.

3️⃣ Vocalisation became an unexpected coping tool
Moaning wasn’t embarrassing - it was regulation.
I felt animal, instinctive, like I dropped into another dimension.
Everything went quiet. I wasn’t “doing” birth anymore - I was inside it.

4️⃣ When I asked for the epidural she was literally minutes away.
The moment I panicked and screamed “I can’t do it” - I started losing my breating, my rhythm. 
But Breathing became everything.
I asked the midwives to speak right next to my ear because I couldn’t hear anything else. Their voices grounded me back into my body.

5️⃣ congratulations. You did it. please take a Quiet skin-to-skin. This matters more than anything
No phones. No questions. No visitors. Mot updating anyone. 
Skin-to-skin wasn’t just bonding - it’s allowing your nervous system settling, slowly returning back to life.

These aren’t universal birth tips.
Just one honest experience of an unmedicated birth, shared gently - in case it helps someone feel more informed, more prepared, or less scared. 🙌🏻

#givingbirth #unmedicatedbirth #naturalbirth #birthtips #newmum

Parenting conversations across 
generations can feel surprisingly hard. 

Many millennial parents aren’t trying 
to prove a point.
They’re just parenting - and still find themselves feeling criticised, dismissed, or misunderstood.

Here’s the psychology behind this ⤵️

Why parenting differences feel personal to older generations:

👉 Parenting is tied to identity
For many older parents, how they raised their children became proof they were “good parents.”
When parenting looks different now, it can feel like a reflection on them…even when no one is criticising. 🤷🏼‍♀️

👉 “Different” can feel like “wrong”
When long-held parenting beliefs are challenged, our brain often responds with defence, not curiosity.

👉 They parented in a different world. 
Less information overload
Fewer conflicting opinions
More certainty about “the right way”

Parenting changes because the world changes rapidly too.

👉 Fear often sits underneath criticism
Fear of losing relevance
Fear of being outdated
Fear that their effort isn’t valued

That discomfort sometimes comes out as judgement even when love is the intention.

If this keeps happening, remember:
It’s often about their identity, not your parenting.

You don’t need to explain or convince.
A calm boundary is enough:

“We’re doing what works for our family.”

This is modern parenting.
And millennial parents are navigating it with more information, more pressure, and more intention than ever.

“Just 3 days and your baby will learn self soothing and independent sleep.” ✨🧚‍♀️

If you’ve been told by a baby sleep consultant that your baby can learn self-soothing in just days with a sleep training program - 
You BETTER continue reading 
⤵️

self-soothing develops over 
YEARS not days or weeks.

What science shows:

🧠 Babies are not born able to regulate stress
Their nervous system is still immature.

🤍 They rely on co-regulation first
Calm develops through repeated, responsive caregiving.

⏳ Regulation unfolds gradually
Through brain maturation, attachment, and safety - over months and years.

🧠 self soothing depends on brain systems that mature much later.
Including the prefrontal cortex, which supports emotional regulation.

Why the term “self soothing” is misleading:

⚠️ It suggests regulation can be taught quickly through a sleep training method.
⚠️ It creates unrealistic expectations for parents.

It works well for marketing.
But biology doesn’t work on promises.

If your baby still needs you to settle, soothe, or fall asleep…that’s not a failure of how your baby sleep.

#babysleep #selfsoothing #sleeptraining #sleepconsultant #babydevelopment

My physical health is not great and my mental health has got worse in the last few months, it wouldn't have been fair to any of us if I kept pushing myself further than I could manage and ended up having to quit suddenly. This way, she's able to look for someone else who's more energetic and is better suited to his needs while I continue doing the school run instead of having to scramble to find someone or take time off work to do it herself.

I'm still very upset about it because he's a lovely child and I've enjoyed our time together so much, but I had to put my health first. I'm hopefully starting with a therapist in the next few weeks, and I'm going to take a little time off from working in childcare to recover before finding a job that's less physically demanding.

Mum has been so lovely about it and I'm so grateful to her for allowing me to be part of her and her son's life. It's always a privilege to be welcomed into a family and trusted with their child or children. We're still going to take him to the playground together every once in a while, and I've said I'm available for ad hoc babysitting if she needs it. I probably won't make any posts for a while until I have a new nanny kid. I know not many people read these posts anyway but it's cathartic to be able to talk into the void and pleasing to know sometimes the void gives me a like in return.

I've been thinking a lot about community lately, and gratitude, and how the things we do include quiet affirmations of care whether we know it or not.

A friend asking me if one of my work kids needs a rain jacket isn't just an attempt to be rid of that jacket. It's a way of saying I love you and I care about the people you care about even if we've never met.

One of my partners chopping the veg and putting everything in pans so all I have to do to make dinner is turn on the hob isn't just giving me a hand with dinner. It's saying I noticed you're tired, and even though I'm tired too I'll use what energy I have to make your life easier. 

My other partner listing the people at a party where I'm not familiar with everyone isn't just helping me to match names to faces. It's saying I know you struggle with faces, and I know you're trying to remember my friends because you care about me, so I'll help you because I care about you too. 

The postie calling out to me on the street to give me a package isn't just doing his job. He's saying I know you, I care about you enough to personally hand you your package when I could have just left it on the doorstep, because you care about me as a human being enough to stop and chat on the street. 

My nanny kid's mum offering me food, checking I'm OK isn't just being a good host. She's saying you're a part of my life, my son's life, and I care about your wellbeing. 

This isn't just a painted rock. It's a symbol of love and care from children I only see every few months, but who think about me when I'm not there as much as I think about them. It's a display of affection from their parents, who could just pay me for the job I'm doing and leave it at that. But they took the time to help their children make this, made the effort to gloss it so the paint doesn't flake off, to give me a physical reminder of the community I've built in the past few years I've lived here.

And from me to the handful of people who read these posts - whether you celebrate Christmas, any other winter holiday, or you're just taking the time to slow down and relax, I hope you get what you want this year.

I have been Very Sick this weekend. It was absolutely miserable. It's likely that I caught it from Signore which means when he was ill on Friday he was feeling all the headache, body aches that I was and wasn't able to verbalise it. We can understand that he's upset by his behaviour, but there's no real way to say with body language "my head feels like a basketball going through a drainpipe". Thankfully mum is smart and empathetic and knows him well enough to guess with amazing accuracy what he needs. Hopefully one day we'll be somewhat as in-tune, but until then I'm learning every day.

In happier news it was his birthday on the weekend, he's a whole 5 years old! He's had a little bit of increase in the recognisable language he uses which is exciting. A lot of kids with delayed language skills have a vocabulary explosion between 5 and 7 years old so I'm hoping he'll learn to express internal feelings. If he never learns to speak the way most people do, it's not the end of the world. He's still a gorgeous happy healthy funny kid. I adore him and worry for him in equal measure.

*TW* for mention of a child being in danger

Signore has recently started running, something he's always enjoyed, but in the past few weeks he's become way faster than he used to. When he is doing something he enjoys, he will not stop until he gets bored of it. He doesn't understand the concept of danger in a very real and terrifying way. The way home from his school is via a very busy main road. These facts combined today and I experienced the most fear I have ever felt in my life.

He's safe, he was never in any real danger, but in my head the 100m to the main road was more like 6ft and I felt real, heart wrenching fear. Since the first day of school mum and I have been reinforcing holding hands crossing roads, trying to encourage him to respond consistently to the word "stop", and generally demonstrating good road safety but right now it feels like none of it has made a dent.

I know once I've slept on it I'll have a dozen ways to change my professional praxis to make sure this never happens again, but right now hours after it happened I still feel scraped raw inside. Some fantastic teachers from a local primary school caught Signore when I yelled to them, and I'm incredibly grateful for their quick actions and genuine kindness. They let us into the office where we (Signore) had a snack while we (I) took a minute to calm down (stop hyperventilating). I will be delivering chocolates next week in thanks. Possibly also jewels and precious spices.

Last week was a bit of a rollercoaster.

Monday was A Bad Day - Signore and I were both overstimulated and overtired, so I didn't read his cues properly until it was too late and he had a meltdown. Frankly, I had a bit of a meltdown too and it was all very stressful. After dropping him home and calming down from the initial "I'm so terrible at this job I should quit" reaction, I realised I could mentally gnaw at the should haves and could haves forever (and kinda did, which messed up my sleep for the rest of the week). Or I could use it to be better next time.

And next time—Wednesday—was better. I made the conscious decision to let go of my preconceived idea of What We're Doing Today. I let him take the lead and only gently nudged him towards the bus stop so by the time he got tired, we were almost there already. We had a picnic, he rode on my shoulders and giggled when I kissed his knees, we chased birds and narrowly avoided disrupting a football game. When we got home he was tired, but not in meltdown territory.

Friday I had to cancel last minute because my sleep schedule was so badly screwed up I was totally brain fogged, and it wouldn't have been safe for me to look after him. It's embarrassing and frustrating to feel like I'm ruled by my disability on days like that, but I'm extremely grateful I have clients who understand and accept my limits. Still working on doing that for myself.

Saturday I had my first 10 hour shift since I started self employment, babysitting an extremely sweet 13mo. It was certainly a lot less stressful to have just one child instead of up to 12 to look after, as is common in nursery work. Even looking after the family dog alongside the baby didn't cause a noticeable increase in difficulty. Baby was not a fan of the heavy metal nursery rhymes I put on (although apparently headbanging is hilarious) so we swapped to generic nursery rhymes and had a dance party after nap time. We hung out in the garden with the dog for a while, and back inside we played "how many dangerous things can I find before Elliott puts them out of my reach?". It's a worldwide game for a reason I guess.

Overall I give last week a "you can do this" out of 10.

Yesterday was a win in my personal/professional improvement project.

I've been making a conscious effort to let go of what others might think and focus solely on the child. It seems basic when I lay it out like that, but I've noticed that I stress a lot about what should be happening—and what counts as acceptable—in my work. But it's often an amorphous blend of past coworkers, parents, things said online, and the concept of people on the street deciding what should be and what's acceptable. Those hypothetical people aren't in my care, they're not professionals, and they're not paying me. They're just weird blobs in my brain trying to make me feel bad and That's Not On.

So when I picked up Signore from his house it was with the plan to go to the playground nearby. There are four different structured places for children to play - a big playground, a little playground, a trim trail type deal, and a larger standalone climbing frame. But when we got to the playground he took off like a mad thing past all of those and headed straight for the low wooden fence that surrounds the carpark.

At first I tried to herd him back to the playgrounds. I offered snacks, juice, even my umbrella (and nearly got my eye punctured for my effort) but he didn't want any of it. He just wanted me to help him balance on the fence. And I realised, why not? Why shouldn't I accept his offer to play, just because it's different to what I imagined? Why shouldn't I hold his hands, help him practice balance and proprioception, catch him when he falls, pretend he's an aeroplane as I carry him across the gaps he's too small to jump? Because someone might judge us for it? Screw that. He's going to be five next month. He'll never be four again, and I'm not going to let his last month of being four be anything less than the fullest it can be.

So we did that for half an hour, and yeah my arms ached but I got to spend time with a kid I adore. We got to be happy and have fun without worrying what strangers might think. We played the way he wanted instead of how we were "supposed to" play, and no one died. It was good. I love my job.

I think my current nanny child (nearly 5yo!) and I have diametrically opposed sensory preferences. This may be a problem but I'm being very brave about it. I like being warm and dry, he loves to jump with both feet into cold puddles that go halfway up his calves. I like having clean, non-greasy, non-sticky hands. He tried to eat the mud at the bottom of a puddle today, and protested loudly when I removed him from said puddle. It is kinda helpful to have the opportunity to exposure myself into being able to tolerate sensory issues for longer periods of time, so I'm grateful to him for that, but dangit kid, stop trying to eat mud. You know there's a snack for you in my bag.

The Uber driver was very nice about having a sopping wet child in her car, so I'm grateful for that too. And Signore's mum took over the showering and cuddling once we got in, which is always a lovely thing to see. She's so in tune with him, and he's so devoted to her it's a genuine pleasure to see them interact. Overall it was a really lovely session and a reminder of how much I love my job.

Next time I see him, I'm going to wear my waterproof trousers on the journey home. I'm hoping he notices and is interested in them because it will give me an opening to incorporate his waterproof coat into play. With any luck, after some play time with the coat at home he'll be interested in actually wearing it, and we can try and minimise the amount of soaked clothing after puddle jumping that I see in the coming months.

Today was a really good day. Signore (almost 5yo nanny kid) is autistic and mostly nonverbal, and I'm still learning to interpret his scripts and vocalisations. I've let my own anxieties about being viewed as a competent care provider bleed into our interactions in the past and after a big meltdown last week I was scared I'd tainted his view of me.

But today, for the first time ever, he actively sought me out to ask me to play with him. Usually he'll respond positively to my additions to his solo play or ignore me entirely. He came to me across the playground and said "help me". He took my hand and led me to the play structure, climbed up the steps and stopped at a corner where there's a fire pole and a slide. I assumed he wanted me to hold him while he went down the fire pole, which is something we've done before, but when I stood under the gap in the play structure he gestured and said "up up". When I climbed up he pulled me to sit down behind him then arranged our bodies so my legs were either side of his body facing the slide. We went down the slide together and I felt like my heart was going to burst with happiness. 

It just goes to show that humans can be incredibly forgiving, and that consistently showing people you're there to help and comfort and support is more important than the mistakes you've made in the past. 

It can be difficult to see the positive when you grow up in an environment where mistakes are brought up over and over. That doesn't mean you have to do the same thing for the rest of your life. You can forgive yourself, and other people will forgive you too. On the bus home he started falling asleep, and when we got off he indicated that he wanted me to carry him. That's very new too; he's very sensitive to touch, and doesn't often permit me to do more than pass a hand through his hair or tickle him a little. I feel privileged he trusts he to carry him home. And yes, my back aches and I think I pulled something in my side. But I'd do it every day if that's what I need to do to make sure he knows I'm there for him.

A month ago I started looking after a new child, and he's taught me so much in such a short amount of time.

He's mostly nonverbal, so I've had to learn to interpret his wants and needs through body language and his unique communication style.

He takes longer to show interest in new things than children I've cared for in the past, and it's taught me to be more patient and slow down.

He enjoys repetition, and it's reminded me that we don't have to keep moving on to something new.

He's almost always moving, which is teaching me to move with him instead of trying to make him stay still. Sometimes he will just stop and his eyes go unfocused like he's listening to a sound I can't hear, and it's helping me to remember everyone has their own world inside their head.

I'm so excited to spend more time with him and learn more about him and myself.

I've recently started teaching myself embroidery, and it's made me think about how a few years ago, my then-3 year old NK ripped a hole in his favourite pyjamas. He was very upset at the idea of throwing them out because he's very particular about his clothes and forms strong attachments to personal items, so his mum messaged me asking if I was any good at sewing.

I said I would do my best, and came over the next morning armed with a brand new travel size sewing kit. Once NK understood I was going to fix his pyjamas he was delighted and wanted to be involved in every step of the process. I gave him the very important jobs of choosing the colour of thread I used, and making sure his baby brother didn't touch any of the sharp pins — both of which he took Very Seriously. He watched in fascination as I threaded the needle and pinned the sides of the rip together, and once it was done he pored over it before telling me "You did a good job, Elliott," which was the highest praise he could think of 😂

After that he'd ask every now and then to see my sewing kit, and informed me each time that "[baby brother] can't touch these [the pins] because they're sharp". It was so lovely to see his happiness over the pyjamas and to know how much he cared about his brother's safety. I still have that little sewing kit in my rucksack - I used it recently to sew up a rip in a well-loved octopus teddy for another former NK, and now I'm using it to fix my hat. Even though I don't see any of those children regularly anymore, the memories associated with them will stay with me long after I've used up all the thread it contains.

Nannying jobs are transient by their nature - children grow up, families move away, new opportunities present themselves. But I'll always have that feeling of pride in "my" kids' growth as people, and that's what really matters.

Trauma is weird. I've made so much progress in the last 10 years, and the last ~5 years especially, mostly due to being surrounded by a network of friends and partners willing to give love and support at the drop of a hat. Also therapy. A lot of therapy.

Today was a good day, objectively. It started off stressful but I managed not to let that set my mood for the day, which anyone who knows me can tell you is a big step forward. I did well at work, made friends with a parent at the school, my current kid is improving his schoolwork and his emotional skills. I even took an uber home even though I didn't "need" to - just last year I would have forced myself to walk because I couldn't afford or didn't deserve such a luxury.

Yet I feel nauseous with guilt right now. Why? Because as a child I was conditioned to be wary of feeling good. The mood of the household depended on the mood of my parent, and at any point laughter could turn into guilty silence after an outburst of anger. I learned to be quiet and walk on eggshells. I'm ashamed to admit I tried to blame my brothers sometimes, because I was so scared of having that anger directed at me.

Winter was the worst, because those grey days meant their Seasonal Affective Disorder was in full swing. Extra sharp mood swings could be triggered by something that was fine yesterday and would be fine again tomorrow. The fact they were likely struggling with depression and anxiety themselves doesn't change the fact that that emotional instability (and the coping mechanisms I developed in response) became carved into my bones. I still can't deal with gloomy rooms and need to have the "big light" on to feel safe in my own home.

How we as adults act around children shapes the rest of their life. Using your child as an emotional stress toy leaves scars, even if you didn't mean to do it. I'll likely never get an apology, seeing as last time I tried to talk to them about it they told me "I'm sorry you chose to be upset by what I said". I'm almost OK with that now. And it feels better knowing I'm doing what I can to make sure the children in my care don't develop scars of their own.
