Work fatigue is not one thing.

That is why so many workers misread it.

You may think you are just tired.

But chronic job stress can show up in different ways:

Mental fatigue — brain fog, overthinking, forgetfulness, decision fatigue.

Emotional fatigue — crying spells, irritability, dread, numbness, anger.

Ethical fatigue — feeling forced to work against your values, silence your concerns, or participate in unsafe conditions.

Physical fatigue — headaches, high blood pressure, muscle pain, insomnia, GI issues, exhaustion.

Spiritual fatigue — feeling disconnected from purpose, calling, faith, identity, or the person you used to be.

This is why the Work Fatigue Quiz™ matters.

It helps identify the level of work fatigue you may be experiencing so you can stop guessing and start moving in the right direction.

Because burnout is not always sudden.

Sometimes it is the result of ignored signals, unassessed stress, and staying too long in an environment your body has been warning you about.

You do not need to wait until your body breaks down to take your work stress seriously.

Before burnout, there is work fatigue.

Take the Work Fatigue Quiz™.

Know your level.
Name what is happening.
Move in the right direction before burnout makes the decision for you.

June is Immigrant Heritage Month — and in New York City, that is not a theme. It is a fact of who we are.⁠
⁠
For more than 400 years, this city has been built by people who came from somewhere else. From the Caribbean, West Africa, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Puerto Rico, China, Ireland, Italy — from every corner of the world — immigrants came to New York and made it the greatest city on earth.⁠
⁠
In District 30, we live that truth every single day. Washington Heights. East Harlem. Harlem. These neighborhoods carry the food, the music, the language, and the spirit of communities that crossed oceans for a better life.⁠
⁠
There are more than 261,000 immigrant-owned businesses in New York State alone — generating $12.6 billion in net business income. This city runs because of immigrant hands, immigrant minds, and immigrant dreams.⁠
⁠
This June, we honor all of them.⁠
⁠
NYC is a city of immigrants. And we are proud of it.⁠

June is Men's Health Month — and this year, we are talking about what too many men are carrying in silence.⁠
⁠
31% of men will experience depression in their lifetime. 9% have daily feelings of anxiety or depression. The suicide rate for men is four times higher than for women.⁠
⁠
But only 1 in 4 ever speaks to a mental health professional.⁠
⁠
That gap is not weakness. It is what happens when we tell men their whole lives that strength means silence. That asking for help is something to be ashamed of.⁠
⁠
It is not.⁠
⁠
To the men of District 30 — the fathers, the sons, the brothers, the neighbors — your mental health matters. Not just when things fall apart. Every day.⁠
⁠
Check in with yourself. Check in on each other. And if you need support, reach out.⁠
⁠
📞 NYC Well: 1-888-NYC-WELL (free, confidential, 24/7)⁠

Senator Cleare is proud to represent a city and a district that has always stood on the right side of this fight. Pride is not just a celebration. It is a declaration. This month, and every month, this office stands with the LGBTQ+ community across Harlem, the Upper West Side, Washington Heights, Hamilton Heights, and every neighborhood in the 30th District.⁠

Took the kids to DC for the weekend. Today, we stopped at the Freedmen House Museum of Alexandria which honors the lives and experiences of the enslaved and free Black people who lived in and were trafficked through Alexandria. On the last floor of the museum there is an exhibit that asks the observer to identify someone that should be recognized for contributing to African American history. Both children, independently of themselves and without influence from me, left cards with my name on it. 

I don't know if they understood what the exhibit was asking or the gravity of what they implied. But that they could experience so much history, in such vivid detail, and think of me as worthy of recognition is an indescribable feeling. Happy Father's Day.

Heart rot. One of the many things that can happen to a fruit tree after it's struck by lightning. I'm saying goodbye to my sweet little peach tree that gave me the best fruit ever until lightning struck it 7 years ago. Even with all my pruning and best attempts, the fruit just rots on the vine. It doesn't have the heart to make the fruit anymore. But the flowers, they are really what its all about. Blooming. It's what comes natural. And I hope the next homeowner realizes that this little traumatized tree is still doing more than its job. It brings beauty into the world, and shade and pollen. And every day, it is still cleansing this dirty air. Over and above. 

Life isn't always about bearing good fruit. Sometimes, all we can do is go through the seasons and just enjoy the cycles. It's enough to bloom, and grow and fade. It's enough to exist planted in the ground, soaking in the sun, making the world around us a bit more lovely. 🍑

Today I walked through an old cemetery on a hill overlooking one of the three rivers that hold this place. Sunlight touched the emerald water below, and the light danced.

One grave stood taller than the rest, marked with a Confederate flag. My brother. A stranger. Someone who died for a cause he may not have chosen. Was he like my own ancestor—who fought for the South in place of a rich man? Was he a survivor too? My ancestor was captured by the North, changed his name, and fought for the North until the war was over, when he came home alive. He didn’t care much about causes. He was too poor.

I’m lucky. I get to live my life for a purpose, not a cause. I’m given time—to understand it, to hold it, to lay it down, and to take it up again with care. I don’t think the man beneath that tall stone had the same choices.

But the river keeps moving. The light keeps finding the water. And I get to keep choosing how I live. I’m glad he has the river. And I’m grateful I can walk past his grave and let the beauty pass through me—reminding me that even here, even now, life keeps offering itself. And every day, I am part of a story still being written.

There was a time when it felt harder to tell good from evil. That doesn’t feel true right now. Political labels don’t really help here — Democrat, Republican, Independent, or Jedi. None of that gets to the heart of it. What matters is how we respond when we’re faced with hatred, violence, or harm.

When racism shows up — in thought, in systems, in speech, in action — it needs to be resisted. Quietly or publicly, internally and externally, but resisted all the same. And the truth needs to be spoken: every person carries inherent dignity. We’re all made in the image of something sacred, whether we name it that way or not. Anything that denies that dignity creates places where damage thrives. Most of us know those places. We’ve all spent time in corners of the world — or of ourselves — that feel impossible to clean up.

Still, we have a choice about how we move through the world. We can lead with love and light, even when it’s difficult. Especially when it’s difficult. It’s harder when we’re tangled up in fear or greed or self-protection — but it’s not impossible. We can do better tomorrow than we did today. And we don’t have to walk that road alone. 

We as a people are better than this. And we can do better.

Exhausted. Greeted the full moon at 3 a.m. Not by choice. But because, for so many creatures, including my daschund, this is the time to frolic. Bunnies bounce across the frosted ground cautiously, but mostly safe. It's a luxury to feel safe, I think to myself. The sky is indigo dotted with faded city stars. Too much light to be truly dark.

My Bella does her business and remains awake until breakfast and while I get ready for work, she sneaks beneath the warm blankets for a long sleep. 

It was the Snow Moon, the one that follows the Wolf Moon. What was it saying in full bloom? I heard it before I fell asleep even, before it rose. Do you recall the story about the empty tomb? Read it again. There were 2 angels there in white, holding the space. Nothing here is truly empty, or dead, or dark.

Too much light, too much light to be truly dark.

I'm in shock tonight, New Year's Eve. Cleaning up my place (as one should - you can't go into the new year all nasty, "like a heathen," as my mom would say. Lol), I opened a manila envelope that's been sitting on my entry table all year. Inside, I found these photos from the 1950s of my grandmother who, when I was growing up, always played jazz gigs on December 31st, even after she had officially retired, all the way until she was in her late 80s. 

I've never seen these photos before, even though I inherited them when she died in 2013. I'm overwhelmed by the symbolism of finding these today, particularly as I think about the year ahead in light of dreams I've had recently that suggest that I have some anxiety about a creative talent that I've been unconsciously ignoring (according to the interpretation of those dreams).

Signal path for the nerds: 

Top row left to right starting at the Boss Tuner > Fuzz Master General Octave Fuzz then the Bit Commander which is a monophonic analog guitar synth> Spatial Delivery for some auto wah & Jerry Garcia tones> Acqueduct Vibrato, (absolutely love that pedal) >White Light (the overdrive pedal that has stayed on the board longest) >Talons high gain overdrive (for a little more sizzle & edge) > Black Ash stone bender for that classic 60s sound > Hoof  for a that germanium/silicone heavy fuzz tone.

Bottom row left to right is the first have of the modulation section with the Grand Orbiter Phaser > The Depths Univibe > Aurelius Chorus > Pyramids Flanger > Silos Delay (with the @oldbloodnoise expression ramper control) >Ledges reverb and end capping with my Boss RC-5 looper pedal.

My baby is 10 months old.
She can drink from a glass, she can take 18 steps all on her own. She winks at me. She loves being chased around. She copies everything we do and noises we make. She can say 3 words but sticks to mama. 

She is the most precious little creature I ever saw. 

Every little hardship that's been, is nothing really.
Birth, breastfeeding, crying, back aches, head aches. It all fades with one look at her.

Everytime she cries a bit too much, I remind myself that it's a hard time being 10 months old and not being able to communicate your wants and needs. But more than that I remind myself that I'm freaking grateful of her existence, and that her crying, whining and wanting to be glued to me, is a part of it. I pick her up and take a second to soak in the moment. To really feel her body against mine. The size of her, her weight in my arms, the smell of her. The way she lean her head against my shoulder. 
I might need my two hands for whatever I'm doing but you know what? I'll make do with one because this is my baby. My Precious little darling girl who wants me to hold her. And I enjoy every bit of it because I know I will wake up one day and she won't ask me to hold her no more. And there will be another day when I won't even be able to. 
There is beauty in that progress too but it also kind of sucks. 
So she can nurse, she can whinge until i have her in my arms again. 
I can sigh and very occasionally find it inconvenient. But it's okay. Because it's temporary. I'll hold her, and I'll cherish it even when I'm dead tired. 
She is already double digits. She is almost a whole year. 

even tho I remind myself daily to soak her in, to enjoy the moment, to cherish her and be grateful for all the good and the less good, time slips through my fingers and memories too. She grows and is a whole new baby every month. I can't believe how little she was just 5 months ago. It feels like yesterday. 

I shed a little tear because I will never hold that little baby in that shape or form again. And I pull my now 10 month old a little closer, hug her tight and remember that she will never be this little again. 
 
! Note; i wrote this almost 4 weeks ago now 😥

She wasn’t just a chef. She was the kind of person who listened when no one else was listening. The kind of person who acted quietly, without the cameras rolling, and without ever needing to be thanked. And now, as she leaves us, I feel like the world deserves to know a little more about the kind of soul we just lost.

During one of her seasons of Worst Cooks in America — I won’t say which one, or who it involved, because this was never meant to be a public story — something deeply human happened behind the scenes.

A fellow cast member was struggling. Really struggling. While filming, her life outside the show was unraveling — she was behind on her car payment, and her home was on the verge of foreclosure. She was trying to stay focused, smile on camera, and keep it together. But in a quiet moment, while talking to her family off to the side, her mic was still on. And Chef Anne heard everything.

Anne didn’t stop to ask production. She didn’t make it a storyline. She didn’t turn it into a teaching moment or a PR stunt.

She just made sure the bills got paid.

The cast member kept her car. She kept her home. And she never had to carry the shame or burden of that moment alone. Anne didn’t want applause. She didn’t ask for repayment. She just knew what the right thing was—and she did it.

That’s the kind of woman Chef Anne Burrell was.

Her talent was undeniable. Her fire, her flair, her humor—sure, the world saw that. But it was her heart that made her unforgettable. A heart that gave without needing credit. A heart that cooked with love, and lived with compassion.

She’s gone now. And maybe not enough people are talking about it. But I am. Because people like that deserve to be remembered.

Rest in peace, Chef Anne. The world may not have known all the lives you touched, but those who did will never forget. #chefanne

Breastfeeding twin toddlers!

We are 2 years, 1 month, 2 weeks and 4 days into our breastfeeding journey. But when will you stop? Seems to be the question society is obsessed with. When they are ready. I fought hard, advocated hard from the very first day the were born and the paediatricians mentioned ‘topping up with formula’ yet they knew I wanted to breastfeed. Mums of twins, triplets and more have to fight extra hard if they want to breastfeed their babies. Because health care professionals; be that paediatricians, GPs, physios, naturopaths,chiropractors, dentists; have little to know knowledge of breastmilk and breastfeeding unless they go out and seek it for themselves (enter @amberley_harris_ 👏🏼)

The amount of terrible and incorrect advice I’ve gotten from well meaning but ill educated HCPs is astounding, and the one that sticks out the most is the paediatrician we were assigned at around 6 months because my twins were not gaining weight as fast as ‘they’ would like. 

Let me tell you, the advice I received from him not only was incorrect, but if I was a mother for the first time or a mother who wasn’t educated on breastfeeding; it literally would have been the beginning of the end of our journey. And it’s crazy because he genuinely believed that what he was saying was true;
“It’s not normal for 6 month olds to feed so often (every 2-3 hours)” WRONG, VERY WRONG!!!

“We see this a lot, it’s hard for your body to make enough milk for TWO babies, you must have low supply” WRONG! If your body can grow and birth two babies and if you have the right knowledge and support, you can absolutely produce enough milk for two (or three or four) babies. Whether you want to or not, is your personal decision, but this was mine. 

“Do you feel full before a feed and empty afterwards” THIS right here was a dead giveaway that he had no clue what he was talking about. At 6 months, your milk production has well and truly regulated and you wouldn’t feel full or empty after every feed ; a soft breast is a healthy breast.

Unpopular opinion? 

I hope not! 

This morning at school the kids were playing on the monkey bars which are a decent height; at least 2m high. And this little boy who would be either 6 or 7, fell. He fell from that height, flat onto his back; so hard that it stunned and winded him. I went straight over to him to see if he was ok, by the time I made it to him he was already moving which made me a bit nervous, so I encouraged him to just sit back down for a minute to catch his breath which he did. Some others came over to see if he was ok as well and we sent a kid to tell the yard duty teacher (who never came 😣😒). 

I could tell he was in pain but he was sucking it up; so people wouldn’t look at him? Or because he’s potentially been told time and time again ‘you’re fine, you’ll be right, get back up’ …. 

I think it’s so important to not downplay it when your child gets hurt. I also don’t think you should make a big song and dance about it either; it’s always taken ALL of my strength, but I pause for a sec before I jump in with Zara (unless it were to be something epic like this was) and sometimes she’s surprised me; she’s been fine and carried on. If she’s hurt though, I go to her and try to be as calm as I can, so that she can ‘borrow’ that calm from me. Teaching kids to suck it up…. I don’t know, I just think it COULD potentially be dangerous. What if this kid had been unlucky enough to have done some spinal damage but he got up and started moving round…. Potentially doing more damage.

For this deeeelicious recipe you will need; 

600g chicken thigh meat
2 TBS olive oil
4 cloves of garlic diced or minced
Brown Onion (optional)
3/4 cup cherry tomatoes 
2 tsp Italian seasoning
1/2 tsp salt
1 cup risoni
2 1/2 cups chicken broth
270ml can of coconut milk (I use Ayam brand) or you could use thickened cream
2 large handfuls of spinach
3/4 cup Parmesan cheese

Cut your chicken thigh into cubes, add olive oil to the frying pan (medium-high heat) and cook the chicken for 3 mins (doesn’t need to be completely cooked at this stage just have the majority of it turn white). Add garlic (you could add a diced brown onion at this stage too if you like), Italian seasoning and salt, cook this for another 4 minutes, add the risoni, chicken stock stir well and let it cook for about 12-15 mins with a lid on, stirring a few times. Once the risoni is cooked, add in that coconut milk, stir and cook for another minute before adding your spinach. Cook that for another minute, then finally add the paresan cheese, stir through and cook for another final minute. I then leave mine for 5-10 mins with the heat off. Serve and enjoy! This serves 4 adult servings with an additional 2 meals for my twins. Zara hasn’t tried this yet, her words were ‘it looks like it might be nice but I think it would be gross for me’. Update on Lolita!

Little Lolita had her vet check-up Friday, and surprise—she’s not an old lady or a former backyard breeder after all! Based on her teeth and gums, she’s likely around 2 years old (maybe even younger). The vet couldn’t tell if she’s had a litter, so it looks like someone lost—or dumped—an unchipped, collarless puppy. That explains her teething and her enthusiastic obsession with Benji!

She’s getting the hang of potty training and often uses the puppy pad, but we’re not 100% there yet. I’m deep in YouTube learning new tricks—reminding me how much easier older, pre-potty-trained dogs are. Lolita’s definitely keeping me on my toes!

When I first found her, she was extremely dehydrated and threw up everything for 24 hours. I gave her small doses of water and a little unflavored Greek yogurt with puréed pumpkin to balance her gut. Thankfully, she’s been keeping her food down for the last 48 hours!

Our first walk with Benji? Let’s just say it was interesting. Lolita has to sprint to keep up with him, so I need to figure out a better system for walking two drastically different-sized pooches! 😳

To keep things safer on the go, I created a puppy lounge in the back of my SUV where she’s strapped into her bed—no more bouncing around like a jumping bean and Benji gets to maintain his own backseat lounge zen! 🧘🏽‍♀️ 

Lolita FINALLY has a collar with her name and my number on it, and her AirTag is on the way. She’s getting chipped and spayed next month (plus her final round of vaccinations). No more nameless, lost puppy—and no chance of contributing to the overwhelming shelter crisis with more pups!

To put things into perspective: The Los Angeles Fire Dept says that firetrucks are designed to handle 3 house fires at once. To keep up with the Palisades and Eaton fires last Wednesday, it would have required 26,000 fire engines, all spraying simultaneously – far more than the entire state of California even has! Even if every water source in the city were running at full capacity, it would have been impossible to supply enough water to fight all of these fires at once.
 
A friend who was caught in the Palisades fire stayed until he was forced to leave at the last possible moment. He told me that he could see several fire tornadoes jumping from house to house as he fled on Wednesday evening. Later that same evening the winds whipped up to nearly 100 miles per hour. So, at once we had both fire tornadoes and fire hurricanes burning through the community.
 
Malibu and the Pacific Palisades have some of the strictest building codes in the country. The Coastal Commission oversees building permits along the California Coast going as far inland as 5-miles in some areas. The Coastal Commission requires stringent fire and earthquake safety precautions in building methods and materials. Even that could not save the homes that were constructed under these strict building requirements (homes built after 2008).

To those saying the city should have done more—yes, perhaps it could have. But in the face of such extreme conditions, even the best efforts would only have delayed the inevitable. This fire was going to be THIS destructive! Man could be no match for mother nature in this case. Let’s hope this is a once in a 100-year freak incident. Unfortunately, we seem to be having once in 100-year freak incidents every single year lately.

There will be much analysis following these fires. There will likely be many more changes and even stricter building codes in the Coastal Commission going forward. I hope it is enough to prevent such a catastrophe in the future. Above all, my heart goes out to the Angelenos who lost their homes and I pray that soon they will ALL be ok.

This is what a 100-mile wind hurricane looks like when it is NOT accompanied by rain, but instead has travelled across a hot desert, collecting tumbleweed and dry brush, before hitting a population that has not seen rain in nearly a year. Just one spark, anywhere in the city, becomes a blowtorch. This is what a perfect storm for fire destruction looks like.

Many want to find blame. No amount of firetrucks, garden hoses and brush clearance could have saved this from happening. I believe the only way we could have better prepared would have been to practically flood the city, dousing homes and hillsides with tens of millions of gallons of water, starting long before the high winds hit our city! But that’s not realistic and likely would not have truly helped anyway.

My heart goes out to all who have lost their homes, their cars and their cherished mementos in this apocalyptic fire. Los Angeles is strong and there is a lot of love here. We will, and already have, come together as a community to help our fellow Angelenos. 

If you are affected, please reach out to your friends and family for help. You are NOT a burden! You ARE cherished citizens of the earth, in need. Many of us feel helpless to aid you in this dire time, but we truly want to. Lean on us over the coming months for strength, help and shelter. 

I send all my love and healing energy your way. You are not alone. 🙏🏽❤️

Just day 2 of school holidays so I wrote a little poem to remind me that yes, parenting small children is fun 🤪

Crumbs in the Carpet

There are dirty handprints all over my walls, and mirrors which look especially bad.  There are crumbs all through the carpet, and bits of dried playdough which drive me mad!  There are clothes all over the floor— an eternal wait to be put back in their place.
Toys scattered all through the house and  more books on the floor than in the bookcase.  There are stains all through the mattresses, and stains all through the sofa.
My makeup’s been taken away to use on the dolls, though hopefully, it can’t go too far.  When I walk in the bathroom, there’s always a puddle of water on the floor.
And when I actually need to go, it seems no one can respect a closed door!  Dishes are piled up in the kitchen, and my condiments have been broken into again.
There’s half-eaten fruit and half-drunk juices lying around—when will the chaos end?  The goal of a clean house just seems like an impossible reality for me,
But does a clean house really mean much, if it’s only achievable when I’m child-free?  The mess and the chaos are signs of little people with imaginations who have fun.
They are signs of a day well-lived, when it’s all said and done.  I can’t expect my home to be spick and span, with no signs of life or living.
I remind myself that I’m blessed by my little people. Tomorrow, I’ll be more forgiving.

What happens when an acupuncture needle is inserted?

At certain acupuncture points, there are neurons that react when mechanically stimulated. This can result in muscle twitches, tingling, heaviness, pressure, or achy sensations.

This reflex triggers the release of Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP), which is a strong vasodilator.

As a result, the blood vessels in the local area widen, increasing the circulation of blood and fluids. This brings in cells and chemicals that have remarkable healing and pain-relieving abilities.

For example:
- White blood cells help the body fight infections and remove debris.
- Red blood cells provide stem cells and promote tissue repair.
- Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) repairs nerve damage.
- Glutamate helps repair cell damage.
- Prostaglandins have anti-inflammatory effects.
- Serotonin helps regulate pain.
- Histamine is a vasodilator and increases cell permeability.

This series of events is known as the local effect, and it has a therapeutic radius of 2.5cm, which is about the size of a nickel.

The most common rotator cuff injury is a tear or strain of the supraspinatus tendon.

The supraspinatus is one of the four muscles that make up the rotator cuff.

The supraspinatus is most commonly affected because it is vulnerable to impingement between the humerus (upper arm bone) and the acromion (part of the shoulder blade).

This condition is commonly caused by repetitive overhead activities, poor posture, muscle imbalances, and shoulder instability.

Some common pain patterns associated with this condition are:

1. Anterior Shoulder Pain: The most common is pain in front of the shoulder, deep in the joint, that sometimes radiates down the arm.

2. Pain with Overhead Activities: Activities that involve raising the arm overhead, such as reaching, lifting, or throwing, may exacerbate the pain.

3. Night Pain: Some may experience pain during sleep, particularly when lying on the affected shoulder.

4. Pain with Arm Movements: Sometimes pain is felt when lifting the arm away from the body, such as reaching out to the side or behind the back.

Here’s how electroacupuncture (EA) & dry needling (DN) can help!

They can help improve shoulder stability by activating inhibited muscles and reducing tension in overactive muscles of the shoulder.

Local EA of the supraspinatus & biceps tendons can help improve blood circulation to those tissues.

This will also reduce pain & inflammation at the impingement site.

Lastly, they help improve shoulder mobility & mechanics. This will help the tissues glide smoothly & reduce the risk of future impingements.

TrPs are knots or bands of tight ropey tissue in muscles.⁣⁣

When pressed on, they are super sensitive and can send pain signals shooting to other parts of the body.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
They can develop for various reasons, but are mostly due to overuse, poor posture, muscle imbalances, or even injuries/inflammation.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

⁣⁣
TrPs often cause chronic discomfort that can be felt locally or in a completely different area from where the knot is located.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Which makes them a huge deal, because they're often misdiagnosed as disorders that require surgeries that don't fix the pain.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
They can also pinch nerves, causing super sharp pains into the arms, legs, feet, and hands.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
TrPs in the neck and shoulders are often the culprits of headaches and migraines.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
We can assist in unraveling those knots with dry needling.⁣⁣

Dry needling the knots causes the muscle to twitch.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Sometimes there’s a dull ache that travels to a distant location of pain.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
This is often  accompanied by release of muscle tension and a comforting warmth or cooling sensation.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Many folks experience immediate relief from dry needling sessions, and after a few rounds, some say their pain completely resolved.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
It's important to note that dry needling is safest when performed by a properly trained and qualified professional.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
If you’re dealing with chronic pain and considering surgery. I highly recommend you seek out a trigger point specialist before doing so.

But she was already a nurse — caring for other people's loved ones every single day at work. Then coming home exhausted and starting all over again for the man she was about to marry.

And then came the misdiagnosis. The hospital visits. Watching him waste away. The uncertainty of not knowing what was really wrong. And the moment she looked at him laying in that hospital bed and asked herself the question that most caregivers are too afraid to say out loud.

That’s something I sit with often.

Myth: Clinical trials and treatments are for everyone.

Truth: They’re not — and that doesn’t mean something is wrong with your loved one.

Cancer treatment is highly individualized. What’s available depends on several factors, including: • the specific diagnosis and stage
• tumor type and location
• genetic and molecular findings
• overall health and prior treatments

Oncological teams aren’t excluding people — they’re matching patients to what’s safest, most effective, and most appropriate for their specific case.
This is why two people can have the “same cancer” and very different treatment paths.

It’s not about fairness.
It’s about precision.
And as a caregiver, understanding this helps you ask better questions, advocate with clarity, and release unnecessary guilt when a treatment option isn’t available.

Knowledge doesn’t remove the fear — but it does reduce the confusion.

This is part of what we do at Baylor Strong: helping caregivers understand the why so you’re not left feeling lost in the process.

Pancreatic cancer is often detected late — not because families aren’t paying attention, but because early detection tools are limited.

This is why radiomics matters.
I learned about this work during a webinar hosted by the Lustgarten Foundation, where I heard directly from the experts leading this research — Dr. Elliot Fishman and Dr. Laura Wood.

Dr. Fishman is advancing radiomics, an approach that combines AI with medical imaging to identify cancer risks that traditional scans can miss. Tumors leave behind patterns — and this technology helps detect those warning signs earlier.

Dr. Wood spoke to the realities of surveillance today — how it’s largely limited to those with hereditary risk or known genetic mutations, even though 90% of pancreatic cancers are sporadic.
This is what caregivers need to know: Research is moving.

Physicians and researchers are fighting.
And the future does not have to look like the past.
We still have work to do — but progress is real, and hope is grounded in action.

When tens of thousands of families are impacted every single year—and that number continues to rise—it does not feel rare to us.
Last year alone, projections estimated 60,000+ new diagnoses. And we already know that number isn’t going down anytime soon.
So this reel isn’t me walking back my frustration.
It’s me adding context.
Pancreatic cancer is labeled “rare” not because researchers or physicians are dismissive—they aren’t. Many of them are fighting relentlessly for better outcomes for our families.

The classification exists because: • Precancerous pancreatic cells don’t always develop into pancreatic cancer
• Researchers can only screen a very limited population, primarily those with known genetic or hereditary risk factors
• There isn’t enough funding to screen the broader population—especially those with no warning signs at all

That means countless people develop pancreatic cancer without being detectable early. And that’s exactly the problem researchers are trying to solve.
This is why they’re working toward: • Earlier detection
• Pancreatic-specific screening tools
• Preventative measures—similar to what exists for breast, colon, and prostate cancer

So yes—“rare” may be the technical classification.
But in living rooms, hospital rooms, and hospice rooms, pancreatic cancer is far too common.
And that tension?

That’s where advocacy lives.
If you’re navigating this journey as a caregiver or family member, visit our website for education, resources, and support created with you in mind. You don’t have to figure this out alone.

💜 Progress is happening. And we will keep pushing.

They still call pancreatic cancer “rare.”
And every time I hear that, it hits a nerve.

Let me be clear — the doctors, researchers, and physicians on the front lines know this disease is urgent. They see it. They fight it. They’re applying for grants, pushing research forward, and doing everything they can with the resources they’re given. They are on our side.

My frustration isn’t with them.
It’s with the way pancreatic cancer is still categorized.
Because when something is labeled “rare,” it creates obstacles — for funding, for research, for the speed at which progress can happen. And families are the ones who feel that delay the most.

And this is the part that infuriates me most:
Pancreatic cancer may be statistically categorized one way in medical journals,
but in real life —
in living rooms,
hospital rooms,
and hospice rooms —
it is far too common.

It’s not rare to the families getting the diagnosis.
It’s not rare to the caregivers holding everything together.

And it’s not rare to those of us living with the aftermath.

So we’re going to keep talking.
We’re going to keep pushing.
And we’re going to keep making noise — because our lived experience matters just as much as the data.

“The newborn will sleep a lot.”🤍

We've all heard it. I've even SAID it. But the reality is a little more nuanced and this nuance often fails to translate when speaking to those yet to have their baby.

Newborn sleep isn’t long, predictable rest. You might get lucky and have a few days of long sleeps straight after birth. Maybe the lactation consultant will even encourage you to wake your baby every four hours for a breastfeed! (that'll hurt!)

But unfortunately these few days, and the myths we're told, tend to lure new parents into a false sense of security. 

Your newborn will likely sleep in short cycles for the whole fourth trimester, with frequent waking, and days that blur into nights.🌙

The issue is when your expectations don’t match that reality, postpartum can feel more overwhelming. It can seem like you're doing something wrong, or that you're not coping like you thought you would. 

But you are not causing your newborn to wake frequently. Most of the time, this is just normal newborn behaviour.

And you're not falling short, just because you're exhausted and overwhelmed. 🫶This is a reasonable reaction to a very extreme set of circumstances for your body and your mind.

✨ Understanding all this helps you prepare differently.
✨ It gives you permission to arrange support in advance.
✨ It softens the pressure you place on yourself.

Slide 1:
“How can I increase my milk supply?” Perhaps the most FAQ in breastfeeding history.

Slide 2:
I’d like to start by recognizing that low supply issues are real, not imagined, and for some mothers, like those with Insufficient Glandular Tissue (IGT), no amount of hydration, supplements or pumping will change that.

Slide 3:
There is also a difference between having low supply and no supply at all. Breastfeeding doesn’t have to be all or nothing. Every. Single. Drop. Counts. Colostrum alone contains millions of immune cells per drop, and mature milk dynamically increases its immune content when you or baby are unwell.

Slide 4:
The reality is that anywhere between 0.1% and 5% of mothers will not be able to produce breast milk at all. Anecdotally, it is estimated that 10 to 15% of mothers may not be able to breastfeed exclusively due to true low supply. The data here is unclear.

Slide 5:
So if you have a true low supply and you want to produce as much milk as your unique body will allow, what can you practically do?

Slide 6:
Perhaps the simplest and most effective method? Allow your baby to use you like a pacifier or dummy. They’re not actually using you, and you’re not a dummy — breasts are nature’s original pacifier.

Slide 7:
The idea that comfort-nursing doesn’t count is a myth. Milk supply is driven by frequency of suckling and breast emptying — the more often a baby is at the breast, the more prolactin is released and the more milk is produced.

Slide 8:
Babies who comfort-nurse are still stimulating your milk supply. In fact, sucking pressure during non-nutritive sucking, when no milk is necessarily flowing at the breast, has been measured as higher than during active milk transfer.

Slide 9:
Comfort nursing 10 or more times in a 24 hour period will not necessarily ensure that every mother who wants to can exclusively breastfeed, but it will support mothers to produce as much milk as is possible for them and their body, in their circumstances.

Slide 10:
I share all of this with a potent reminder that a deep, comfortable, effective latch is vital for removing milk from your breasts. The best way for you and your baby to achieve this is with in-person support from an IBCLC.

Slide 11:

# The Things I Promise My Boys — Carousel

## SLIDE 1 — Hook

**I’m a boy mum.**
**For life.**

Two of them now.
Here’s what I promise them.

*(Visual note: biggest, simplest slide. This is the scroll-stopper. Plain
background, bold type. A photo of you — bump, or you and Farai — works well here.)*

-----

## SLIDE 2

**An opinion — never the right to impose it.**

I promise to teach them they may think what they like about anything,
and force it on no one. A view held loudly is still just a view.

-----

## SLIDE 3

**No means no. Full stop.**

Not “no for now.” Not “no until I whine, push and outlast you.”
A no is a closed door. You do not stand outside it negotiating.

*(Visual note: give this slide the most weight — boldest treatment, most
white space. It’s the strongest line in the set.)*

-----

## SLIDE 4

**Privilege is just a fact about the room.**

Some doors will open for them with less force than others must use.
The right response isn’t guilt — it’s using your voice
in the rooms where others were handed a quieter one.

-----

## SLIDE 5

**They will learn about periods.**

And about the invisible, unthanked labour of mothering —
the nights, the mental load, the body never quite returned.
Not so they pity women. So they *see*.

-----

## SLIDE 6

**Their body is theirs. No one else’s belongs to them.**

Not a partner’s. Not a stranger’s. Not mine.
I fed them from my own body — that was a gift I *chose* to give.
It was love. It was never their entitlement.

-----

## SLIDE 7

**A family is a lifelong, equal responsibility.**

Not “helping.” Not babysitting their own children.
Equal — all the way down to the parts no one claps for.

-----

## SLIDE 8

**Real generosity.**

The kind that walks into a room, notices quickly
who has been handed less — and quietly evens it.

-----

## SLIDE 9 — The turn

**I’m not raising them to be good *for* women.**

I’m raising them to be whole.
And a whole man cannot stand the sight
of someone smaller being made smaller still.

I already see it in my eldest. Seven years old, fierce about fairness.
He made me braver. His brother is coming into a home
where all of this is already true.

-----

## SLIDE 10 — Close

**Two boys.**
**One mother who will not budge.**

What a privilege. What a responsibility. What a joy.

*(Visual note: mirror Slide 1’s style so the carousel bookends. Add your CTA
here or keep the CTA only in the caption — don’t crowd the slide.)*

-----

-----

## CAPTION

So. It’s official. I’m a boy mum — for life.

Two of them now. The one who made me a mother seven years ago, and the one I’m carrying as I write this — due in the height of summer.

And somewhere between the scan and the school run, I started making them promises. Not the soft kind. The kind I intend to keep even when it’s inconvenient. *Especially* when it’s inconvenient.

I learned young how to comply. I am still, as a grown woman, unlearning it. My sons will learn the opposite skill — and it starts with the promises in these slides. ⬆️

I’m not raising my boys to be good *for* women. I’m raising them to be whole — and a whole man simply cannot stand the sight of someone smaller being made smaller still.

I already see it in my eldest. He came into this world and made me braver. He is the reason I learned to hold a boundary, to trust my gut, to stop apologising for taking up space. His brother is coming into a home where all of that is already true.

Two boys. One mother who will not budge on any of it.

What a privilege. What a responsibility. What a joy.

Last week, a major publication, @theeconomist, told millions of women that their bodies might simply be unable to feed their babies. The figure they leaned on: 10 to 15%, sounded authoritative. Final. Scientific.

So I went and read the research (again) for myself. Had there been another pivotal study published since I had done the research for myself own book? 

That number isn’t wrong, exactly, but it isn’t true in the way it’s being presented either. It appears in review papers as something “believed” or “estimated” - and when you trace it back, it doesn’t lead to a single robust study of the wider population. Not one. It leads to a figure that’s been repeated so often it began to sound like fact.

Underneath it all are three very different truths that have been conflated and folded into one: 
women who perceive low supply
women with a low measurement taken in small self-selected studies
and women with genuine, biological primary insufficiency. 

Those are not the same group. Treating them as one inflates the fear and blurs the facts.

I want to be really clear about something, because it matters: primary lactation insufficiency is real. Some women genuinely cannot produce a full supply and they deserve proper diagnoses, real clinical support and zero judgement. I will always hold space for every one 🙏🏽

But most of the women reading this? Your struggles in those early weeks were far more likely about support, information and a rocky start, not an underlying biological/physiological issue. 

This is what I want this little corner of the internet to be. A place where we don’t accept fear dressed up as fact. Where we ask who a headline serves before we let it live in our heads? Where mothers are trusted with the full picture, caveats and all - not simply handed a verdict.

You were never the problem, mama. But the narrative you were given was.

If this reframed something for you, send it to a mother who needs to read it today. Because empowerment comes from facts + support, not scaremongering headlines.

How long does it take for your period to return after birth? 
Can you get pregnant whilst breastfeeding? 
Why hasn’t my period come back postpartum?

These are some of the most searched questions in early motherhood. And they are some of the most common ones in my inbox too. So what's the answer? 

Breastfeeding suppresses ovulation through prolactin and its effect on the HPO axis (the hormone loop that runs your cycle). But the timeline of your period returning varies enormously from woman to woman and the science still has HUGE gaps in it.

I think those gaps are grossly unfair. We deserve clear answers about our own bodies. But where the data falls short, we can still use what we do have to inform us, to steady us and to make decisions from a place of knowledge rather than fear:

If your period has returned sooner than you’d hoped, I send you love. I understand firsthand what that feels like.

And if it hasn’t yet - and you are longing to conceive again, you may be wondering whether you need to stop breastfeeding to make that happen?

Before you decide, I want to gently remind you of something. Eight out of ten mothers in the UK stop breastfeeding before they want to. In the US, around six out of ten stop exclusive breastfeeding within the first three months. I share this not to scare you, but to reframe the question.

Do you need to race to wean in order to conceive as soon as possible? Or can you, for now, focus on the child already in your arms and allow nature to take its course?

That decision is entirely yours. There is no wrong answer. I would simply encourage you to sit with it, journal on it and give it space before making any big change.

Let’s set the record straight...Breast milk doesn’t magically stop being protective at 6 months! 🤪

It adapts. It strengthens. It intensifies.

🦠 Immune protection?
Breast milk contains live leukocytes - immune cells that increase in concentration when baby or mother is sick. These cells don’t vanish after infancy. They rise when they’re needed most.
(Riskin et al., 2012)

🧠 Brain development?
Breast milk provides DHA and other critical fatty acids long into early childhood - when the brain is still wiring itself at lightning speed.
By age 5, the brain is 90% of its adult size.
(Dewey, 2001; Victora et al., 2016)

🦷 Jaw, teeth, and airway health?
The act of breastfeeding promotes healthy jaw growth, proper tongue function, and better alignment of the palate and teeth.
It reduces the risk of malocclusion and future orthodontic issues.
(Peres et al., 2015; Viggiano et al., 2004)

💗 Emotional regulation and resilience?
Breastfeeding supports co-regulation, lowers cortisol, and fosters secure attachment - especially in highly sensitive or neurodivergent children.
(Jansen et al., 2008)

🌱 Independence?
Children who are allowed to self-wean on their own timeline often become more independent, not less.
Because when safety is internalised, confidence grows.
(Dettwyler, 2004)

So no - the benefits of breastfeeding don’t “tail off.”
They evolve.
They deepen.
They rise to meet the child - and the moment.

The only thing that wanes with time?
The public’s tolerance for breastfeeding beyond infancy.

And that says more about society than it does about science.

With love,
Danielle

Slide 1
“But if I just give him the boob, he’ll stop crying,”
This used to live rent free in my mind every time I considered weaning/night weaning ⬆️
Slide 2
And you know what? It WAS easier.
In the moment.
But what about the 47th time that day? What about at 3am? What about when I was so touched out my skin was crawling and I felt like a terrible mother for resenting the thing that was supposed to be beautiful?
Slide 3
The real question I was asking myself wasn’t “How do I get my toddler to stop asking to nurse?”
The real question was: “How do I say no without breaking their heart?”
Because THAT’S what kept me stuck.
Slide 4
I wasn’t nursing 10+ times a day because I didn’t know I could stop. I was doing it because every time I tried to set a boundary, my child sobbed like I’d betrayed him. And the guilt was unbearable. So I’d whip my boob out. Again. Even though my body was screaming for respite.
Slide 5
Here’s what nobody told me: The reason “Just say no sweetly and offer a snack instead,” didn’t work wasn’t because my child was manipulative or I was doing it wrong. It’s because we had nothing to bridge the gap left by not nursing, yet. Boob = comfort. No boob = no comfort, PANIC
Slide 6
So when I’d say “not right now, darling” & he’d scream harder…I thought: “See? This is cruel. I’m hurting my rainbow baby.”
And I’d cave.
And the cycle continued.
And I got more touched out.
And more resentful & more guilty for feeling resentful.
Slide 7
But what was actually happening was that I hadn’t taught him that “No boob,” doesn’t mean, “No love.”
I hadn’t given him the tools to ask for what they actually needed (which was CONNECTION, not milk).
I hadn’t shown him I could hold a boundary & hold him emotionally; nobody had taught me how.
Slide 8
The draconian parenting advice said: “Just stop. Let him cry himself to sleep. He’ll learn.”
The alternative: “Honor his needs for as long as he wants to nurse. Your discomfort doesn’t matter.”
Both felt wrong to me…
But I didn’t know what to do instead?

And so I turned inwards & drew upon:
• My MSc in Psychology

Weaning with Love teaches:
• How to say no without your child feeling abandoned.
• How to hold a boundary with love, when they cry
• Understanding the need beneath the desire to nurse…
All whilst preserving & deepening your bond

accessibility_caption:
Advice about the safety of drinking alcohol whilst breastfeeding varies widely depending upon the source. You may find yourself bombarded with conflicting information about whether a glass of bubbles or a few beers are safe for you to consume as a breastfeeding mother. You might have heard from a friend that it is totally fine to breastfeed after a few drinks, but you have almost certainly also heard that you need to pump and dump your milk after consuming alcohol. So what are the facts? Is it safe to have a glass of wine or two whilst breastfeeding? If so, how much? Does alcohol get into your milk supply - and is there ever a need to pump and dump after a drink? 



The NHS, advises nursing and pumping mothers that, "An occasional drink is unlikely to harm your baby, especially if you wait at least 2 hours after having a drink before feeding...Regularly drinking above the recommended limits can be harmful for you and your baby." (1) The American Academy of Pediatrics has similar advice, adding that alcohol can impact milk production (2). These recommendations are based upon the fact that it takes around two hours after the consumption of alcohol for your blood alcohol levels to return to zero as a breastfeeding mother. If you choose to consume alcohol whilst breastfeeding, it is worth knowing that your blood alcohol levels peak after around 30-60 minutes, or 60 - 90 minutes if consumed with food (4). So if you want to minimise the amount of alcohol passed onto your nursling through your milk, it would be best to nurse them either as you are drinking an alcoholic beverage or an several hours after doing so.  



Does Alcohol Pass into my Milk?



In short, the answer is yes - in tiny quantities. For example, if a 75kg woman were to consume six glasses of wine in quick succession, my blood alcohol level would peak at 0.17% (5). If I were to then breastfeed my baby, 5-6% of that alcohol would be passed on through my milk. This would mean that it would contain 0.01% alcohol. To put that into context, orange juice has an ABV measure of 0.07% (6). It is also with knowing that alcohol passes into and out of your milk freely as your body metabolizes it. Therefore, there is no need to pump and dump simply because you have had a glass of bubbles at a party. If you were to consume large amounts of alcohol, it would be advisable to wait at least a few hours until your blood alcohol levels were lower before nursing or pumping for your baby. 



Whilst the amount of alcohol in your breast milk may be your primary concern as a nursing or pumping mama, it should not be the only consideration. For instance, if you choose to consume alcohol whilst breastfeeding, it is important to remember that you cannot safely bedshare with your baby after doing so (7). Additionally, it is likely that after multiple alcoholic drinks, you will feel tipsy or even drunk. In this case, your ability to care for your baby could be compromised because of the risks of falling and so on. Whilst it may well be safe for you to nurse your little one after a drink, caring for them safely could be the greater challenge. With this in mind, planning for another loving caregiver to look after your child after a particularly merry night out is advisable.

Did you know that by having your tea/coffee as the first thing you drink/eat for the day actually doesn’t support helping to keep you functional in the day? Here’s why: 

If you’re someone having your supplements with your tea/coffee first thing in the morning you’re actually preventing essential vitamins and minerals from being absorbed in the body from both supplement and food sources. 

Tea and Coffees contain polyphenols and tannins that bind to iron in the gut 
forming complexes your body can’t absorb. This mainly affects non-heme iron (the type in plant foods and most supplements). Drinking tea or coffee with iron can reduce absorption between 40–80% of both heme based and non heme based iron. 

If you then add cows milk, it can make it worse for iron because milk contains  calcium which competes with iron for absorption in the intestine by another 20-40%.
Other supplements such as vitamin D, zinc and magnesium are also affected by milk based tea/coffee drinks but not as significantly as iron. Still if you’re on a list of supplements that you need to support your body for your concern, separating the time between your meals & supplements with the time you have that first tea/coffee if key. Try and wait at least 2 hours between meal and supplement consumption and also pair your supplement intake with vitamin C especially for iron absorption.

Additionally drinking caffeine on an empty stomach increases cortisol (your stress hormone) and further triggers a blood sugar spike. This happens because caffeine stimulates the release of adrenaline and signals the liver to release glucose into the bloodstream. For some people, this can lead to:
• energy crashes later in the day
• increased cravings for sugar or carbs
• feeling jittery or anxious
• disrupted appetite and mood
A simple fix: is food that is high in protein, fibre and healthy fats FIRST. This helps slow glucose release and keeps your energy more stable throughout the day.

What you'll need: 
- Milk chocolate melts (i used 1 pack but i would use 2 after making this it turned out I didn't have enough chocolate to fully coat them all) 
-Fresh dates 
-1 jar of pistachio paste 
- Filo pastry 
- Coconut oil 
-optional dried roses to top the chocolate 

Pit your dates and slice on one side not fully so you can open them up but they're still connected.
To make kataifi get some of your filo pastry (I literally measured with my heart) and about 2 heaped tbsp of your coconut oil heated and chuck in your chopped up filo cook it till golden brown. You can crush it a little more afterwards too if it's still too big. 
Warm up your pistachio paste for 30sec in microwave and mix your pistachio paste with your cooked filo (now kataifi)
Pop it in the fridge for a bit to set then scoop about a teaspoon in each of your dates and pop back in the fridge again to continue setting. 
Melt your chocolate, pull our your combined dates and coat them in the chocolate(add your roses here before they set to much). Let it set fully in the fridge for about 20mins 

Enjoy!

This post deserves 2 days worth of Christmas, because there is nothing worse than family members or friends you are catching up with who have no idea of the journey you have been going through, asking intrusive and insensitive questions like “so when are you having kids?” “When are you going to give us another baby?” “When am I having grandkids?”

Setting clear and respectful boundaries is a healthy way to protect yours and your partners emotional well-being.

1.Set expectations early on- Even if it’s a group or individual text message to someone you know would ask.  “Before we talk about anything, I just want to mention that we’re not in a place to discuss the topic of our fertility (struggles). I hope you can respect that.”

2. Direct but gentle response “I appreciate your concern, but we’d prefer not to talk about our fertility journey right now. It’s something we’re working through privately.”

3. Change the subject “I know you mean well, but I’m not ready to discuss that. Let’s talk about something else—how have you been doing lately?”

4. Express need for privacy “We’ve decided to keep our fertility journey private for now. It’s a personal topic for us, and we’d appreciate your understanding.”

5. Be honest about your emotional state “That’s something that’s been really tough for us, and talking about it can be difficult right now. I hope you understand.”

6. Redirect the question “We’re still figuring things out, but I’d love to hear what’s new with you! Any exciting news on your end?”

Tips for Maintaining Boundaries:
* Be Consistent: You may have to gently repeat yourself a few times. People often forget or don’t realize how uncomfortable their questions can be.
* Stay Calm: It’s okay to feel frustrated, but try to keep a calm tone to avoid conflict. You have every right to protect your privacy.
* Know When to Step Back: If someone is pushing you repeatedly or not respecting your boundaries, it may be necessary to limit or pause communication for a while to protect your mental health.
It’s completely okay to set these boundaries, and doing so can help you maintain emotional and mental well-being during such a sensitive time

Folate: The Key to Fertility & a Healthy Pregnancy 🌱
When it comes to fertility and pregnancy, folate (vitamin B9) is essential for both mom and baby! It plays a critical role in DNA synthesis, cell division, and most importantly, the formation of the spinal cord and neural tube—key areas of early fetal development. Adequate folate intake helps prevent birth defects like spina bifida and supports healthy fetal growth.

However, not all folate is created equal! 🌿 Methylated folate and folinic acid are the most bioavailable forms of folate, meaning they are easily absorbed and utilized by your body. In contrast, folic acid (the synthetic form) can be harder for some people to metabolize and has been shown to be less effective, potentially even detrimental during pregnancy. Opt for methylated folate or folinic acid in your supplement for optimal support in your fertility and pregnancy journey! 💚

Additionally, natural forms of folate can be found in foods such as: 
- Eggs
- mangoes
- Beetroot 
- Avocados
- Leafy greens like spinach kale broccoli
- Beans chickpeas and edamame
- Lentils 
- Pawpaw (papaya)
- Bananas 
- Citrus fruits 
- Nuts: almonds, pistachios, walnuts & cashews
- Seeds: sunflower, sesame, flax, chia, pumpkin

🩺 The Science-Backed Benefits of a 10-Minute Walk After Meals 🚶‍♂️

Taking a short walk—just 10 minutes after eating—is a simple habit that can have a surprisingly positive impact on your health. Research continues to show that light physical activity after meals supports multiple aspects of wellbeing. Here’s how:

🔹 Improves digestion: Gentle movement helps stimulate the digestive system, allowing food to move through the stomach more efficiently and reducing bloating or discomfort.

🔹 Regulates blood sugar levels: A post-meal walk can help muscles absorb glucose from the bloodstream, leading to smaller blood sugar spikes—especially beneficial for those managing diabetes or insulin resistance.

🔹 Enhances cardiovascular health: Regular short walks support healthy circulation, lower blood pressure, and improve overall heart function.

🔹 Boosts energy and mood: Walking increases oxygen flow and endorphin release, reducing fatigue and improving mental clarity.

Even a 10-minute walk after each meal adds up to 30 minutes of light activity a day—an easy, accessible way to support long-term health.

The Synthetic Presence

Our history is a ledger of linen and lace, but what if a new, impossible fiber had been birthed in a forgotten corner of the 18th century? She poses with the solemn dignity of tradition, her mourning attire of velvet and silk anchored to the earth. Yet, beside her, draped in shadows of strange reflections, lies the element.

This object, molded by a future that did not yet belong to her, should not exist there. And yet, it does. Had our chronology integrated this strange, imperishable form with the era of steam and corsets, would romance have remained the same? Would the fragile beauty of the moment have surrendered to the eternity of the polymer?

A portrait where classical beauty is haunted by a fictional strangeness, questioning whether what we see is a distorted memory or a reality we simply chose to forget.

Children are not born knowing war.
They arrive with open hands,
ready to receive the world —
not its ruins.
No child draws battlefields in their first notebook.
They draw houses.
Huge suns.
Flowers that believe the earth is kind.
If we truly fought for the future,
every child would have peace first.
The greatest victory of humanity
will be the day we choose to protect children
more fiercely than we protect our wars.

But no one warned us they would begin to walk among us.
Not with thunder.
Not with swords.
But with quiet eyes that refuse to look away.
They say they go to war to defend the future of our children —
yet children are always the first to fall.

while truths are buried deeper than the bodies.

Because love is the first form of protection.
Because unity is the oldest rebellion.
Because awareness cannot be bombed into silence.
In a world that feeds on fear,
their tenderness is radical.
They do not shout.
They do not march.
They simply stand — together.
And somehow, their presence
reveals everything.

The Sanctuary Within
“Hell is empty, and all the devils are here.” Never have Shakespeare’s words echoed with such haunting truth.
We wander through turbulent shadows,
Where light is named darkness, and malice wears the mask of grace.
Our moral compass has shattered against the jagged rocks of survival,
Leaving the act of kindness as a rare, almost forbidden fruit—
A virtue that delivers us into the arms of silence and solitude.
No sacred ritual, no hollow prayer can bridge this divide.
To those who wait for a distant God to descend from the clouds:
Look inward, for the Divine breathes within your own chest.
There is no absolution found in stone or sky,
Only in the quiet pulse of our deeds,
In the mercy of a clear conscience and a spirit at peace.
I would embrace the humblest poverty before I bartered my soul;
For the flesh is but a fleeting whisper, a gift of borrowed time,
But the soul is an eternal flame that outlasts the stars.
Peace be upon the beings of light who walk beside me—
Fellow travelers in this brief, beautiful, and perilous journey.

Diary of an October: Day 33 (November 2nd)

The Echo of the ‘Pão por Deus’.

The forced stillness of Day 1 dissolves into a day of historical echoes. Today, children run with cheerful baskets, enacting a ritual that, in its current form, barely recalls its brutal origin: the “Pão por Deus” (Bread for God’s Sake).
This day is not merely the continuation of the previous month’s weight; it is the reminder of past suffering, etched into the collective memory. I see the faces of yesteryear, soiled with dirt and coal, their feet bare on the cold ground, where the begged bread was literally the only barrier against extreme hunger.
The purity of the children’s eyes, confronted with the harshness of existence. Today’s simple request is yesterday’s cry for survival. This image haunts me: the awareness that, behind our current abundance, lies the trace of lives where charity was the thin line separating life from death.
May this day, which still carries the heavy burden of necessity, teach us the real difference between the lightness of consumption and the gravity of compassion. May our abundance always be an act of memory.

Diary of an October: Day 32 (November 1st)

The Weight of Continuation.

Today, the calendar tells us the page has turned, yet the soul recognizes the deceit. The heavy curtain of October insists on smothering this new dawn. November 1st: All Souls’ Day. It is a day less of memory and more of a performance by the restless souls, whose frequencies, now unleashed, collide with our plane.

Sometimes, the greatest wisdom is withdrawal. I do not seek direct confrontation with this creeping weight, for I know the risk it carries. The solution is not to fight the external shadows, but to create an internal structure of light they cannot penetrate.

I fold my hands not in supplication, but in containment. On this day, my breath becomes a ritual: I seek the absolute stillness and silence of my essence, transforming worry into focus. The only energy I allow myself to attract is that of stoic peace. I pray for the light of my ancestors, that they may continue in peace wherever they are. May the storm of memory and the threshold pass, finding my soul firm and untouched.

While the exterior adorns itself with the mask of its non-essence, I, in the profound silence of my dwelling, recline in the penumbra of this day’s end. This stillness mirrors the ultimate truth of October: the solemn closing of the cycle, the moment to seal the doors. This is not a refuge forged by apprehension, but rather an imperative of spiritual preservation.

I seek the deepest silence so that my consciousness remains undisturbed by the world’s performance. Today, vigilance is my sole companion, and the wait for November is my only purpose. Diary of an October: Day 29 (The Vigil)

October always descends as a heavy month, and perhaps this is the very reason I chose to chronicle these days—in the profound hope of altering the established pattern.
This has historically been the month when the most sombre company attempts to overrule my will, subtly diverting my destiny hour by hour, day by day. Misfortunes seem to succeed one another, serving only to remind me that I must perpetually elevate my consciousness so that the light of my very being might repel these ill spirits.
I undertake this task daily, yet I cannot escape the chilling sensation that the darkness touches the soul during our most vulnerable moments, those times when our guard falters. I live this month in a state of vigilance, prepared to contend with the worst, ready to subsist entirely upon the spiritual integrity granted to me by the Creator.

Diary of an October: Day 28 
Today, the day had no color. The landscape revealed itself as a mirror to the inner world: sand beneath a sky threatening to collapse at any moment. I sit in the vast, desolate stillness, not to rest, but to finally confront the storm—not the one brewing in the dark clouds above, but the one churning relentlessly in my chest.
In this solitude of the dunes, where there are no landmarks and no refuge, the only remaining structure is the naked truth. The weight of the fabric I wear is the burden of convention, of expectations that insist on shackling the spirit, but the wind speaks a different language.
Life sometimes demands this posture: to face the darkest horizon, to refuse to yield a single step to the threat of chaos, and to find firmness at the very root of one’s being. The fear is there, but the only way to overcome it is to acknowledge it and sit alongside it, beneath the changing sky.

Diary of an October: Day 27

Today, the veil of the coming storm. The sea breeze kisses the skin, raising goosebumps not from cold, but from a profound awareness of the power surrounding me. I walk the edge of the world, where the land meets the abyss of the ocean, and the clouds bear the weight of ancient secrets.
There are no masks here. The attire that cloaks me, with its layered sweetness, contrasts with the rawness of the setting, revealing an intrinsic duality: the delicacy of the self before the untamable vastness.

Diary of an October: Day 26 (The Scrutiny)
Today, I utterly challenge the narrative. I defy any who would vouch for the stories they parrot without ever subjecting them to question.

I defy those who blindly follow the findings of scientific studies without first asking: Who paid for this knowledge?

I defy all those lingering in the educational system, compelled to regurgitate the same tired subject matter taught a hundred years ago. I challenge the very historians to prove that the vast majority of their content is not, in its essence, a carefully crafted fiction. I even challenge those who transcribed, translated, inverted, and re-penned the sacred Scripture, thus steadily distancing us from the Creator.

I challenge the very controllers of this reality to reveal themselves as they are, and not as they are described. Today, I sever my binding connection to the mental program installed since my earliest consciousness. I free myself from that control by way of the narrative.

I have lost friends and family to suicide …. Forever in our hearts …

 She found herself on the floor of her bedroom clutching the belt and the coat hanger…
She got lucky…

She crashed her car and stepped away unharmed,

So, if you can be anything in this world,  be kind…

Ghee originated in India and has been used there for thousands of years.

Ghee is cultured, clarified butter (the milk solids and water are removed leaving just the fat). 

Ayurvedically, ghee is used extensively in cooking and therapeutic applications, both internally and externally, as the best medium for delivering Ayurvedic formulations.

- Aids digestion 

- Is nourishing, strengthening, immunity building

- Is anti-inflammatory and rich in linoleic acid, Vitamins (A, K2, and E), and Omega-3 fatty acids. And it’s a source of butyrate acid, a short-chain fatty acid that promotes gut health.

- Heals the gut and supports the liver, heart, and kidneys

- It is good for mental health conditions, and improves brain health, concentration, cognitive function, intelligence, and memory.

** Although a source of dairy, it is very well tolerated by many people intolerant to dairy due to the milk solids being removed.

The most important words on any food packaging are the words written after the word INGREDIENTS: - it doesn’t matter what pretty colours or fancy words are used on the front of the package, just remember that is all MARKETING!!! Those words are used to sell the product, it doesn’t mean that’s actually what is in the product. Check out this packet I found of NATURAL, ORGANIC MONK FRUIT alternative to processed cane sugar. Based on the packaging, I expected to see the ingredients as 100% monk fruit, but no… 99% erythritol and only 1% monk fruit!!!! And there is no where on the packet that shows the certified organic symbol so therefore it’s used just as marketing - it’s not organic at all! What are you really buying?? Read the back, not the front!

UCP Seguin is proud to be part of the They Deserve More coalition. Due to TDMs tireless advocacy, gains were again made for people with disabilities in Illinois and for those that care for them!

Illinois lawmakers delivered wins for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities this legislative session, even in a challenging budget year.

 ✅A $0.60/hour Direct Support Professional (DSP) wage increase, raising the state reimbursement rate to $21.90/hour, or 146% of Illinois' minimum wage.
 ✅A transition to a "zero-hour" staffing model in Community Integrated Living Arrangements (CILAs). State leaders committed to implementing this change in a way that maintains service hours for at-home day programs and other daytime CILA supports.

These results are thanks to your advocacy to state legislators throughout the spring. Now, it’s important to thank them for responding. They Deserve More is sending a group thank you letter to all state legislators, and we want you to be part of it! Click the link below to add your name.

Shirley Perez of @thearcofillinois shares an important reminder. The PUNS database is more than a waitlist. It helps the state government and IDD advocates  understand and respond to the needs of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

Thousands of families face uncertainty in the PUNS process. Some are waiting for funding, some cannot access services, and others are not even registered in the system.

Even when a family’s funding is approved, services are not guaranteed. Too often, they can’t find a provider because the DSP workforce is stretched too thin.

Real solutions start with investing in trained, dedicated staff.

The curfew debate is loud. The teenagers are louder.

Washington expanded curfew zones to Navy Yard and U Street this year. Officials framed it as a safety measure. Teenagers across the city responded with a different diagnosis: the problem is not what time young people are outside. The problem is that there is nowhere for them to go.

At the District's Teen Summit this spring, students spoke directly about mental health, stress, safety, and how disconnected they feel from the people making decisions about their lives. Large public gatherings, they explained, are often less about causing problems and more about finding connection in a city that can feel isolating.

Many neighborhoods lack consistent recreation spaces, youth-focused alternatives, or affordable activities. Advocates argue that investing in arts programs, mental health support, sports access, and career development would create a larger long-term impact than stricter enforcement.

One drop of water. One smartphone. One minute.

Researchers at Germany's Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing have built a rapid contamination test that detects fecal contamination in water using a single drop, a 3D-printed smartphone attachment, and the phone's own camera.

The technology reads urobilin, a natural byproduct of hemoglobin breakdown that traces human or animal waste in water. It was validated on real river samples and at a Berlin wastewater treatment plant. It works in complex field conditions, no lab required, no 24-hour wait, no specialized equipment.

For the communities living without reliable clean water access, in disaster zones, in regions where a municipal testing system does not reach, this is what accessible public health looks like: diagnostics in your pocket.

Takashi Tateishi and Manami Matsumae!

Takashi Tateishi is one of the sound team members who engaged in a sort of "secret deal" made possible by close workspace arrangements. During a slump in Mega Man 2 composition, Manami Matsumae contributed eight bars to Air Man's stage theme because her workspace was next to Tateishi's. Tateishi would later return the favor by composing the Forest Stronghold theme, a fan favorite, for U.N. Squadron. Yoshihiro Sakaguchi, who acted as their manager, was aware of these and other instances from other sound members.

3do had some interesting music, a lot of it was orchestrated with real instruments or symphonic sounding keyboard patches, bc it was one of the first systems with CD Rom, allowing streaming audio straight of the disc, so less games had digital programmed chip music.  But this also caused quite a bit of jumping around the disc and frequent soundtrack interruptions/graphics glitches and system crashes.  Some of the discs would play as a cd starting at track 2.  Or maybe mine was just old and crusty.  Anyway 3do history is important because the games were so bad they’re good, and the starting price of the system was way too high and then it just crashed after PS1 dropped, lol.  Now the physical games with the original long boxes are rare/collectible and the whole thing is one of the quirkiest stories of vgm lore.  I used to find the loose game discs in a stack of uncased cds for $1 each at Take2 in the strip mall over there….

The Safer Together plan reflects the important principles that long-term community safety depends on upstream prevention and action on root causes, and not only on emergency response and enforcement. VCC supports the continuation of the Free Fare Zone and the expansion of deeply affordable transit for all Calgarians.

5 things I didn’t do in the first 5 days postpartum 

🛌 I didn’t leave my bed

Being in bed facilitates rest. It becomes your safe space. Your nest.

It’s where healing happens. Where you prioritise skin to skin and feed around the clock without distraction. Away from the visual pull of everything that “needs” doing.

Five days in the bed, five days on the bed, five days around the bed — the 5/5/5 rule should be a bare minimum.

🥗 I didn’t eat cold or raw food or drink cold drinks

Warmth supports healing. After birth your body is repairing tissue, rebalancing hormones, establishing milk supply, restoring blood.

Cold food requires more digestive effort when your body needs to prioritise recovery.

Warm broths, stewed fruit, congee and slow-cooked meals support circulation and digestion without adding extra work.

🚿 I didn’t wash my hair

There is something powerful about the natural scent of early postpartum — the warm, milky smell of your body and your baby.

Oxytocin is heightened in those early days and scent plays a role in bonding. Strong fragrances can mask those natural cues. The same applies to scented body wash, deodorant and perfumes. Especially in those early days, be mindful of synthetic fragrances — and gently share that with visitors too.

🧣 I didn’t let my belly go unsupported

After birth your organs are finding their way back into place. Everything feels open and tender.

Wrapping the belly provides containment, eases discomfort and supports healing.

🛁 I didn’t bath my babies

Babies aren’t dirty. They arrive coated in vernix, which supports their skin barrier and early microbiome.

Delaying bathing supports temperature stability and breastfeeding initiation. In those early days, skin to skin and sleepy warmth matter most.
